articles.title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research
articles.body:
This post discusses a public METR report on AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic. I did not work on this project or see the unredacted report.1 All opinions are my own and do not represent METR or the report authors.
Thanks to Ryan Greenblatt for discussion, feedback, and help with modeling, and Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, and Hjalmar Wjik for comments.
Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026), say this threshold will be met when:
- They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D.2
- This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs.3
For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed.4
The report authors found that:
- Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative."
- While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted.
This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack. Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team) have projected.
Researchers must be sped up a whole lot
Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.
Researchers work on improving algorithms and architectures; Anthropic has sometimes referred to these innovations as “compute multipliers.”5 Overall AI capabilities (“effective compute”) is the product of compute multipliers and training compute. Because the compute multipliers are only one input into capabilities, this means that if AI capabilities are advancing twice as fast overall because of software progress, the rate of growth in compute multipliers would need to be more than twice as fast: perhaps ~2.5-3x faster based on reasonable assumptions.6 Since there’s uncertainty about the size of speedup and how much of it comes from AI, I’ll go with ~2-3x.
Similarly, researcher labor is only one input to discovering these compute multipliers: they need to test their ideas, which requires compute for experiments. If we assume a very simple Cobb-Douglas model where experiment compute and labor are similarly important, that means the uplift to labor roughly needs to be the square of the acceleration in compute multipliers.7 This would imply that we would need a (~2-3x)^2 = ~4-9x speed up in labor to make overall AI capabilities go twice as fast.8
However, once capabilities start speeding up significantly, this also means that low-hanging fruit is plucked at a correspondingly faster rate. Each new compute multiplier takes more and more work to discover and implement (i.e., “ideas are getting harder to find”). Before there was much acceleration from AI, labor roughly grew at some roughly fixed exponential rate from hiring more humans. Combined with growth in compute, this compensated for diminishing returns enough to maintain the baseline rate of capabilities progress. But to maintain a new faster rate of capabilities progress without scaling compute faster, we would need a new faster rate of growth in overall labor.
Since the human labor force is stuck growing at more or less the old rate, the uplift from AI would need to get larger and larger over time just to sustain capabilities progress at its new rate. That means the uplift today, after several months of accelerated progress from AI,9 needs to be even higher than ~4-9x, the estimate for what it would take to double progress at the start: maybe the necessary labor uplift is ~10x. This is very uncertain, and substantially more or less is plausible. But it lines up surprisingly well with informal self-reports from Anthropic staff, who say they are now getting a ~12x uplift from the use of internal models.
When you’re picturing a 10x uplift, you should not be imagining that every researcher is now a team of ten researchers — as anyone who has ever done anything knows, a team of ten does not get ten times as much valuable work done per hour as one person. Instead, it’s as if every researcher at Anthropic is in a time warp bubble where they experience ten days for every day that passes in the outside world. As if AI lets them think, read, speak, type, and do everything else ten times faster.10 Anthropic probably wouldn’t have been able to speed up its research this much by hiring any number of people.11
This could compound on itself extremely rapidly
A reasonable default expectation is that as AI capabilities continue to improve, AI researchers will be sped up more and more from automation: if today it takes them a month to get as much work done as they used to in a year, soon it will take a week, and then perhaps a day. If this increasing labor uplift is strong enough to overcome diminishing returns, then in the absence of other bottlenecks it would translate into even larger speed ups in the rate of AI progress: progress will start going 4x faster, and then 8x, and then 16x, and so on.
The report authors were very uncertain about this question, and say that their picture changed several times with new information. But ultimately, they did not find evidence of bottlenecks or steep diminishing returns that would get in the way of compounding acceleration.12 They also report seeing some (confusing) redacted evidence indicating that acceleration could already be above 2x and increasing over time.
If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year. It seems that around a year’s worth of AI progress got us from modest acceleration to the point where AIs now make AI progress roughly twice as fast. If acceleration from AI is smoothly increasing, then at this new rate, we should expect that we will double the rate of progress again within six months. At that point, it would take three months to double it again, then six weeks.13
In theory, these doubling times would add up to infinite capabilities within one year. In reality, at some point we would reach the effective ceiling on software efficiency. But I expect these limits to be very far from where we are now.
If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict. If these systems were seriously misaligned, I think they would likely disempower humanity, and this could lead to human extinction.
The industry is not prepared to handle this safely
The “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” is such an important and extreme milestone because it is a strong concrete indicator of extreme capabilities in the very near term. Indeed, in an earlier version of Anthropic’s RSP (May 2025), the highest named risk threshold for AI research automation (AI R&D-5) corresponded to a somewhat weaker milestone.14 According to the old RSP, Anthropic would be required to have, at a minimum, security good enough to “protect against model-weight theft by state-level adversaries”15 by the time it reached AI R&D-5.
I agree that very strong security, both for model weights and algorithmic secrets themselves, is a minimum prerequisite for undergoing an intelligence explosion next year without running very large risks of killing billions of people. The AI industry is nowhere near this bar: both OpenAI and Anthropic recently had major security breaches by amateur groups. Beyond strong model weight security, I also think we would need robust logging and monitoring with universal coverage, reliable measurements of monitorability, effective countermeasures against monitor collusion, principled alignment training techniques with very convincing model organisms or interpretability to understand how well they’re working, governance infrastructure for pacing progress if we notice these alignment and control interventions start to break down…and many other measures if we’re going to approach an intelligence explosion in anything like a responsible way.
Unfortunately, most of the important evidence that fed into these conclusions has been redacted from this report. Analytical choices will inevitably be fraught, and the report authors say that the evidence was often confusing.
I trust that my colleagues did a careful and rigorous job navigating making sense of what they saw, and I made a big update based on this report. But I wish much more of the underlying evidence was transparent so readers don’t have to rely on trust. We may be running out of time to get on the same page about timelines and takeoff speeds, and it is much harder to do that when external scientists cannot examine the data and test out their own models.
Because I may have seen other confidential information that might be relevant to timelines and takeoff speeds, I will only discuss implications of public evidence rather than sharing precise bottom line forecasts.
The precise condition is: “We observe or expect double the rate of progress in AI aggregate capabilities compared to both the rate we’d expect and the fastest rate of extended progress we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D.” 
My understanding is the reason to have both of these conditions (double the rate of progress both compared to the counterfactual and compared to the fastest sustained rate without much AI assistance) is to exclude cases where the pace of capabilities would have slowed down a lot without AI automation, but we manage to keep the old trends going with dramatic uplift from AI.
The precise condition is: “It is plausible that this doubling is significantly attributable to the automation of research and/or engineering (as opposed to other factors, such as increased headcount, compute, or general productivity), such that continuation of the trend in AI progress seems likely to lead to even greater acceleration.”
The definition of the threshold is a bit finicky, partly because two speedup conditions must be met (speedup relative to the counterfactual and speedup relative to the past). But on a plain reading, my best guess is that it has been met. 
The authors of the METR report estimated roughly a doubling in the rate of progress relative to the past, but they only attribute roughly 80% of the current speed-up to AI, which would mean the central estimate for observed speedup relative to no AI was roughly ~1.8x as of the time of writing their report, in October 2026. 
But they also found that the contribution of AI has been growing over time, and I would guess that now (as of November 2026) it is appreciably higher. Even if the rate of progress is not fully double the counterfactual right this second, the threshold incorporates reasonable expectations (“We observe or expect double the rate of progress…”).
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei explains the idea of compute multipliers in this essay: “The field is constantly coming up with ideas, large and small, that make things more effective or efficient: it could be an improvement to the architecture of the model (a tweak to the basic Transformer architecture that all of today’s models use) or simply a way of running the model more efficiently on the underlying hardware. New generations of hardware also have the same effect. What this typically does is shift the curve: if the innovation is a 2x “compute multiplier” (CM), then it allows you to get 40% on a coding task for $5M instead of $10M; or 60% for $50M instead of $100M, etc. Every frontier AI company regularly discovers many of these CM’s: frequently small ones (~1.2x), sometimes medium-sized ones (~2x), and every once in a while very large ones (~10x).”
Common formulations of Cobb-Douglas often measure labor as the number of humans. In that formulation, there needs to be a parallelization penalty on top of labor and the coefficients don’t add to 1. As I discuss below, I’m choosing to represent labor in terms of serial labor acceleration rather than the number of humans; this formulation was suggested by Ryan Greenblatt in this post.
To make the math simple, I just assumed that labor and experiment compute contributed equally (i.e. compute multipliers = (labor)^0.5 * (compute)^0.5. This means you square the acceleration in compute multipliers to back out the acceleration in labor. The range I gave omits uncertainty on the size of the contributions: for example if labor contributed ⅔, you would instead need to raise it to the power of 3/2.
I say several months rather than a full year because the report authors say that the initial faster progress in late 2025 was in significant part due to other factors, though the current speedup is mainly due to AI.
In practice, the 10x uplift is unlikely to be uniform: some tasks (e.g. more “hill-climbable” tasks) will be sped up much more than others, for a net productivity improvement as big as a 10x uniform acceleration.
That is, any number of people that actually exist. I’d guess it would be sufficient if you could clone all the existing researchers several hundred times, but there aren’t that many strong AI researchers and engineers in the world.
From the report: “A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.”
This heuristic argument is consistent with simple but plausible models where recursive self-improvement makes the rate of AI progress exponential in cumulative AI progress (e.g., log effective compute); here is a derivation of this heuristic argument for one parametrization of this class of models.
AI R&D-5 was defined as: “The ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling. Specifically, this would be the case if we observed or projected an increase in the effective training compute of the world’s most capable model that, over the course of a year, was equivalent to two years of the average rate of progress during the period of early 2018 to early 2024. We roughly estimate that the 2018-2024 average scaleup was around 35x per year, so this would imply an actual or projected one-year scaleup of 35^2 = ~1000x.” It is weaker because it compares to the fixed 2018-2024 period rather than the fastest observed pace without significant AI acceleration, and it doesn’t technically require that you do any attribution to AI to meet the threshold.
The minimum commitment was to reach RAND’s ASL-4 security level; my understanding is that this is a level of security that would protect model weights from a routine operation by top state actors (e.g., China), but not from a top-priority operation. This is how Anthropic describes it: “At minimum, the ASL-4 Security Standard (which would protect against model-weight theft by state-level adversaries) is required, although we expect a higher security standard may be required.”

That is, any number of people that actually exist. I’d guess it would be sufficient if you could clone all the existing researchers several hundred times, but there aren’t that many strong AI researchers and engineers in the world.
From the report: “A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.”
This heuristic argument is consistent with simple but plausible models where recursive self-improvement makes the rate of AI progress exponential in cumulative AI progress (e.g., log effective compute); here is a derivation of this heuristic argument for one parametrization of this class of models.
AI R&D-5 was defined as: “The ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling. Specifically, this would be the case if we observed or projected an increase in the effective training compute of the world’s most capable model that, over the course of a year, was equivalent to two years of the average rate of progress during the period of early 2018 to early 2024. The minimum commitment was to reach RAND’s ASL-4 security level; my understanding is that this is a level of security that would protect model weights from a routine operation by top state actors (e.g., China), but not from a top-priority operation. This is how Anthropic describes it: “At minimum, the ASL-4 Security Standard (which would protect against model-weight theft by state-level adversaries) is required, although we expect a higher security standard may be required.”

articles.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
articles.body:
Firecracker is supposed to keep untrusted code inside a microVM. We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host.
We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH.
PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup.
00 / Choosing where to take control
A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. Firecracker documents this arrangement in its architecture overview.
The call that runs the virtual CPU looks like this:
ioctl(vcpu_fd, KVM_RUN, 0);
While the thread is in that system call, the host kernel holds its saved userspace registers in a structure called pt_regs. These registers describe the Firecracker thread: its instruction pointer says where execution should resume, and its stack pointer says which userspace stack it should use.
That made the return from KVM_RUN an attractive target. If we could locate and modify the saved frame, we could choose the code Firecracker executed when the thread returned to userspace. A guest operation that caused such a return would provide the trigger.
We already had access to selected host physical memory through a guest mapping. To use it, we needed to identify the Firecracker process, find code we could call in that process, and locate the register frame belonging to its active vCPU thread. The starting point was a page of memory we controlled inside the guest.
Figure 1. The guest identifies its Firecracker process, finds the saved registers for a vCPU thread, and redirects the thread when it returns from KVM.
01 / Finding our guest page on the host
The guest and host use different physical address spaces. A page has a guest physical address, or GPA, inside the VM and a host physical address, or HPA, in the machine backing it. On the target, Extended Page Tables (EPT) provide the translation between them.
We placed a recognizable byte pattern, a nonce, in a guest page. The first resolver took that page's known GPA and its contents as inputs. Together, they gave us an address to translate and a way to check whether the translation reached our page.
The resolver searched the host physical ranges covered by the memory primitive for candidate EPT roots. An EPT root is the starting point of the translation tables. For each candidate, the resolver followed the entries selected by the guest address until it reached a physical page, then checked that page for the nonce.
The snippets below are explanatory pseudocode with descriptive helper names. They show the data passed between stages and the checks used to connect them.
for root in candidate_ept_roots:
page_hpa = walk_ept(root, guest_gpa)
if page_hpa is invalid:
continue
contents = read_host(page_hpa, length(nonce))
if contents == nonce:
candidates.append((root, page_hpa))
The nonce check connected a proposed translation to memory we controlled. The broader search produced two candidates; validation of the nested page tables reduced them to one EPT root. Walking that root gave us the host physical address of our guest page.
We called this result guest_page_hpa and passed it to the next resolver. We now had a recognizable object in host memory. The next task was finding the host process that mapped it.
02 / Finding the Firecracker process
Firecracker maps memory used by the guest into its own address space. That mapping gave us a way to work backward from the guest page to the process.
Host processes use page tables to translate their virtual addresses into physical memory. The top level is called the page global directory, or PGD. Recovering the appropriate PGD would let us translate addresses inside Firecracker and read its code and stack through the memory primitive.
Our reverse mapper searched the native host page tables for a mapping of guest_page_hpa. A normal page table walk starts with a virtual address and produces a physical address. Here, we looked for a mapping to a physical page we already knew, then recovered the virtual address and page table root associated with it.
The check runs in both directions:
for mapping in reverse_map_host_page_tables(guest_page_hpa):
pgd = mapping.root
guest_page_va = mapping.virtual_address
resolved_hpa = walk_host_page_tables(pgd, guest_page_va)
if resolved_hpa != guest_page_hpa:
continue
if read_host(resolved_hpa, length(nonce)) != nonce:
continue
process_candidates.append((pgd, guest_page_va))
This connected the host process's virtual mapping to the physical page found through EPT. The reverse mapper returned one validated address space. We retained its root as host_pgd and used it to inspect the process.
The next resolver looked for the Firecracker executable in those mappings. It identified an ELF image and checked a known byte sequence in Firecracker's write(2) wrapper. That connected the recovered address space to the binary we were targeting.
ASLR changes where an executable is loaded. The difference between an address in the ELF image and its corresponding runtime address is the load bias. Once the mapper had identified the image, it could recover that bias and use it to locate the code required by the exploit:
The mapper returned the load bias as firecracker_base. With that value and host_pgd, we could locate code in the running process, translate its virtual address to host physical memory, and compare the bytes there with the expected binary.
We checked three locations: the write(2) wrapper that would produce our proof, the continuation after the KVM ioctl, and a short xor eax,eax; ret sequence needed to return cleanly. Their purposes become relevant when we construct the return path below.
At this point, the guest could inspect the Firecracker image and its private mappings. We still needed the saved registers of the thread currently running our VM.
Figure 2. The nonce identifies the guest page in host memory. Its mapping leads to a host page table root, which lets the next resolver locate and validate the Firecracker image.
03 / Locating the live vCPU frame
The frame finder took host_pgd and firecracker_base from the preceding stages. It used them to recognize the host thread's saved state.
The most useful clue was the return address. A vCPU thread in KVM_RUN should have a saved instruction pointer at the corresponding ioctl continuation in Firecracker. We could calculate that address from the validated binary and its load bias.
We then searched host memory for a pt_regs frame consistent with that call. An address match alone would also pick up stale stack contents, so the candidate had to satisfy several related checks:
The stack check tied the frame to the same address space we had recovered from the guest page. The instruction and caller addresses tied it to the Firecracker image. The syscall fields tied it to the operation running the vCPU.
The search left one candidate. Its location was stored as frame_hpa, the host physical address of the saved register frame. We passed it, the PGD, and the load bias to the final helper.
Before changing memory, the helper repeated the code signature, frame, and stack checks. This ensured that the active stage used the same process state the resolvers had identified. The subsequent execution and recovery checks would establish that the selected frame was live.
Figure 3. The candidate register frame must agree with the KVM ioctl, the recovered process page tables, and the validated Firecracker code.
04 / Redirecting the return from KVM
We chose a simple payload: make the Firecracker process write a recognizable string to its own stderr. This would give the host runner an observable result from the process we had taken over.
The string was N8V23M2\n, seven characters followed by a newline. It occupies eight bytes and fits in one stack word. The call we wanted Firecracker to execute was:
write(2, "N8V23M2\n", 8);
Here 2 is Firecracker's stderr file descriptor. The buffer pointer must refer to the string in Firecracker's address space, so we stored the string on its private userspace stack.
We saved three stack words before modifying them. One held the string; the other two held the return addresses for the temporary call sequence. We then changed the saved register frame to supply the wrapper address, its arguments, and a stack pointer for that sequence:
RIP = address of Firecracker's write wrapper
RDI = 2
RSI = virtual address of the marker on Firecracker's stack
RDX = 8
RSP = virtual address of the temporary return sequence
Returning from write also needed care. A successful write of eight bytes returns 8, while a successful KVM_RUN call returns zero. We placed the address of xor eax,eax; ret first in the return sequence. It clears the return value before the second address brings execution back to Firecracker's original ioctl continuation.
The resulting control flow was:
KVM_RUN returns to userspace
-> Firecracker's write wrapper emits the marker
-> xor eax,eax; ret sets the return value to zero
-> execution resumes at the original ioctl continuation
With the stack and saved registers prepared, the guest wrote one byte to its serial port. That operation caused the vCPU thread to return from KVM_RUN. The kernel restored the modified registers, and Firecracker entered the write wrapper with our arguments.
The wrapper emitted the marker, the return sequence cleared eax, and the thread rejoined its original execution path. After control returned to the guest, the helper restored all three stack words.
Figure 4. The saved register frame enters the write wrapper. Two return addresses lead through the return-value adjustment and back into the original Firecracker path.
05 / Checking execution and recovery
The host runner captured Firecracker's stderr separately from the guest. The complete output was:
N8V23M2
The capture contained exactly eight bytes, including the final newline. Firecracker was still running, guest SSH was responsive, and the helper had restored the three temporary stack words.
We checked recovery with a fresh pass that made no memory changes. It was given the same frame address and repeated the register, code, and stack checks after the trigger. The checks passed, and it found no stale marker in the temporary stack location.
These observations answered three different questions. The guest log recorded the trigger and restoration. The host capture showed that Firecracker executed the selected operation. The final validation checked the state after execution.
Figure 5. The guest log, Firecracker stderr capture, and final validation record the trigger, host execution, and restored state.
06 / Root execution on the host
By the time the marker appeared, the guest had selected the host thread's instruction pointer, function arguments, stack data, and return path. Firecracker executed the call using its own privileges.
The target was Firecracker v1.16.1 on x86-64, with host kernel 7.0.0-1011-aws and guest kernel 6.18.44+. We launched Firecracker directly as root under systemd-run and pinned it with taskset. Consequently, the controlled call executed as root on the host.
The existing write wrapper gave us a compact proof of that control. Extending it to other calls would require choosing code and arguments compatible with the process's mappings and syscall policy.
The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM.
The address discovery is what lets the exploit follow the running instance. The EPT resolver connects a guest page to host memory; the reverse mapper recovers the host address space; the image mapper locates Firecracker under ASLR; and the frame finder identifies the vCPU's saved state. Adapting the final stage to another build requires validating that binary's code signatures and return path.
The guest had used access to host memory to take over the thread running the VM itself. A serial write supplied the trigger, and the next userspace operation belonged to us.
Captured resolver values and artifacts
The following values come from the preserved execution record. The methods above use symbolic names so that the role of each value is clear; this table connects those names to the recorded addresses.
The records use run ID eventpath-v23-0907self02 and boot ID 2b3cd5ac-2311-427f-a50a-6a79ecb8daa7. These identifiers connect the resolver records, host capture, and validation after restoration.
The earlier memory provider also received host-selected task and canary page frame numbers as independent validation overlays after constructing the memory aperture. Those addresses were not consumed by the EPT resolver, reverse mapper, Firecracker mapper, frame finder, or final marker helper.
The release bundle contains the final helper source, JSONL resolver records, host capture, recovery manifest, four preserved read-only resolver binaries with provenance, and SHA-256 manifests. The final helper accepts the PGD, load bias, and frame HPA produced by the resolvers. Its checks cover the run identifier, address ranges, code signatures, saved registers, and stack geometry; its dry-run mode performs validation without writing memory.

articles.title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
articles.body:
China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.
China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips.
Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.
The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

articles.title: Zelda is back and better than ever
articles.body:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 151, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, get psyched because it’s officially Bad Holiday Movie Season, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
Zelda is back and better than ever
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Godzilla is back too, a couple of new phone accessories, and the best pen in the world.
This week, I’ve been reading about Andrew Garfield and GTA VI and sexy joke thieves, finally actually watching The Sopranosfor the first time (I know, I know), mourning the end of Salon, reinstalling the new and extremely improved Notion Calendar, testing the new Keurig Alta coffee machine, reviewing the iPad Mini and the touchscreen MacBook Pro, and really thinking about just throwing it all away and buying an Enough Phone.
I also have for you the long-awaited return of a classic Zelda game, a monster movie worth the trek to the theater, a couple of great new phone accessories, awesome retro headphones, and more. Let’s do it.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / playing / listening to / hacking onto an E Ink display this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. I have a confession to make: I’ve never played this game all the way through. Not sure how! Just missed it. But seeing my friends and coworkers fall back in love with Hyrule has convinced me to get all the way into the remake. I genuinely can’t wait.
- Godzilla Minus Zero. Three years ago, Godzilla Minus One was a big hit and a surprisingly great movie. The sequel came with much higher expectations, but everyone seems to agree it’s a deserving follow-up. I’m not generally one for monster movies, but this series really does it for me.
- Affinity for iPad. Canva’s app now unifies all its tools in one place, just like on the Mac. Affinity makes perfect sense on the iPad, and comes with lots of Apple Pencil integration and clever touch-friendly tools. I’m no designer, but I am excited to play with this as a photo editing tool.
- The Moft Dynamic Folio Case. Here’s one for all you iPhone Duo buyers. Moft’s cases are a little complicated to figure out, but really cleverly designed to make your phone even more useful. I’m guessing this is going to be a lot better than Apple’s weird case / kickstand thing.
- The Peak Design Kickstand Travel Battery. While we’re on the subject of kickstands, here’s the one I’m buying this week. Peak Design makes good stuff, and I frequently find that I need extra juice at exactly the moment I want to watch something on a plane or train. This one’s going right into my backpack and probably never coming out.
- The Bambu Lab H3C. I am dangerously close to becoming a 3D Printer Dude. At $2,500, this one’s a little steep for my wallet, but I think my colleague Sean Hollister is right that this is what the future of 3D printing looks like. Simpler, more foolproof, easy enough even for a goofus like me to make some pretty cool stuff.
- “Ranking the world’s most popular pens for journaling.” I know we all love a good pen — and Peter McKinnon does an excellent job of breaking down a few dozen supposedly good pens to see which ones really hold up. I bought more than one pen after watching this.
- Instagram Edits for Mac. Oh, great, just as I was finally getting good at CapCut! I like the Edits mobile app a lot, and the desktop app seems to be even a little more powerful. Plus: free. This is how I finally take down Cristiano Ronaldo.
- The Sony MDR-3R headphones. Respect to Sony for taking the retro headphone trend all the way to its logical conclusion and just releasing the headphones from the original Walkman. You’ll look a little like Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything when you wear them, and $60 ain’t cheap, but there’s something so incredibly ’70s-era cool about them.
- The Motorola Signature 27. This is just a pure tour de force of a smartphone spec sheet. Monster camera; brightest screen; giant battery. Also very cool to see a flagship phone with support for GrapheneOS, for the less Google-inclined among us. It’s expensive, and only shipping… someday… but I just like that phones like this exist.
We talked last week about Readwise Books, the new app that’s a mix of Kindle, Goodreads, and Strava. I’m a longtime fan and user of Readwise Reader, so I wasn’t shocked that I liked the new app a lot, too. And I’ve heard from a bunch of you that you do, too!
I’ve talked to Tristan Homsi, one of the Readwise cofounders, a few times over the years, and have always enjoyed hearing his thoughts about reading, apps, and digital products in general. I asked him to share his homescreen to see if I might be able to get a hint about what he’s reading and the other stuff he thinks is good. (I also asked Daniel Doyon, Readwise’s other cofounder, to share, and he didn’t respond. Daniel is dead to me.)
Here’s Tristan’s homescreen, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: iPhone 13 (!).Believe it or not, I chose to buy this relatively outdated phone last year… not because it’s my favorite form factor or anything, but because it’s closer in specs to the median device our Readwise users have and helps me build a bit more user empathy with them. I’m able to catch performance regressions and bugs in Readwise that the developers on our team with Duos and Pro Maxes and such miss.
Let me tell you though, iOS 26 itself does not work amazingly on an iPhone 13. Lots of lagging and janky animations. I am somewhat bought into the conspiracy theory that they make the old phones suck so you buy a new one… not so much intentionally, but rather by virtue of just making each successive iOS use more and more resources, doing fancier and fancier things.
The wallpaper: My lovely wife and my cat Sophie :)
The apps: Clock, Settings, Google Calendar, Camera, Google Maps, Spotify, Bay Wheels, Oura, Eight Sleep, Auto Eight, BeReal, ChatGPT, Runmeter, Strava, Readwise Highlights, Readwise Reader, Phone, Messages, Safari.
Of course, I have all three Readwise apps front and center. Highlights and Reader as app icons, and Readwise Books in widget form at the top! It’s a great reminder to jump back into your current book (I’m reading Apple in China right now… speaking of Apple!) instead of scrolling twitter (on a later page), and seeing my friends currently reading really makes me want to jump in and join them :)
I also am a huge fan of the somewhat-defunct social app BeReal. It had its moment in 2022, but quite a few of my friends are still on there! You post once a day, can see what your close friends around the world are doing, and most importantly can’t get sucked in for more than two minutes since it limits you to a random photo or two a day! I still post basically every day, and have almost five years of memories in there.
Speaking of getting sucked in, I don’t have it pictured on my home screen, but I also have Clearspace installed, which helps me stay off of all social media.
Some other apps shown on the homescreen: “auto eight” is something I vibecoded to better control my Eight Sleep mattress (lol)… Strava and Runmeter are awesome for tracking my runs… and Bay Wheels is my main mode of commute around San Francisco daily.
I also asked Tristan to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
- I follow some amazing niche internet blogs, which you should check out if you haven’t. I love the blog Slime Mold Time Mold, famous for their citizen science and potato-maxxing. I also love Gwern.net, Deepfates, and Dynomight… among many others!
- And of course I’m always reading books. The most recent fiction series I loved was the Red Knight series — which I can only recommend if you are into dense, dark, fantasy — but man, if you are, the author is a genius.
- For non-fiction, it’s hard for me to plug anything but my favorite book of all time, The Beginning of Infinity. It’s not the easiest to get through, but if you do it will likely change the way you see the world, as it did for me!
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Finally started reading Dungeon Crawler Carl (recommend); finding the Duo to be a perfect foldable reading device. Going to have to take a break to save Princess Zelda though.” — Will
“I’m playing around with CutWire’s Drift video editor (alt to CapCut) and I’m honestly shocked at how high-quality it feels.” — Kolin
“A wonderful Belgian developer put together an alternative Kobo EPUB reader called Kobalt that I’ve been really enjoying. It’s got a very clean and well-designed UI with a bunch of really nice features that make it a much more enjoyable experience to use. There’s even an Android app, so I also put it on my Supernote Manta to use with larger format content. So much nicer than KOReader!” — Dylan
“As a mourning Arc user, I’ve been on the search for my next browser, especially one with a good mobile experience and this one is AWESOME. Lens Browser feels like what Arc Search on mobile would have become had they stuck with it. Currently only mobile for now, but it does have a Mac toolbar companion for sharing links.” — Garrett
“Since Arc Search is going away, I’ve been using Lens, and it’s exactly what I’ve been wanting in a mobile browser. It’s the perfect Arc Search replacement.” — Corey
“My Boox Picco literally just arrived today. So now I’m trying to churn through Fellowship of the Ring on it, plus my economics textbook.” — Lukas
“I’m trying to get back to the gym, and my motivation is I can only watch a show I want to watch if I’m on the treadmill. I’m finally starting Barry. Turns out, good show!” — Ben
“Well, Zelda..., but also World of Warcraft Forever, but also 007 First Light (which is letting everyone play the opening for free).” — djstarburst
“Playing the Final Fantasy Resonance demo on Switch 2 while waiting for Ocarina of Time to show up at my door and having a blast. It’s not spectacular, but hits the right amount of nostalgia and gameplay for me.” — Micheal
“Been catching up on Avatar: Seven Havens, and oh my goodness, the art style, the characters, the music, the worldbuilding!!!??? It’s all so fresh and delightful and human!” — Olof
Signing off
I’ve mentioned Kagi a bunch of times in this newsletter — it has been my default search engine for the last few years, and I can’t recommend it highly enough. (What if Google, but good, you know?) The challenge with Kagi is it costs $10 a month, which is a lot to ask when Google is free. But as of this week, you can now at least try it for yourself, since Kagi will give you 50 free searches before even asking you to sign up. You get 100 more when you do, even before you pay.
If you search a lot, and miss what Google used to be, give Kagi a whirl. I am a very happy customer, and suspect I will be for a long time.
See you next week!

articles.title: Cryosphere Faces Permanent Damage When World Overshoots 1.5C, Scientists Warn
articles.body:
Cryosphere Faces Permanent Damage When World Overshoots 1.5C, Scientists Warn 46
			
		 	
				A UN-backed report warns that even temporarily overshooting the Paris agreement's 1.5C warming target could cause permanent and widespread losses of glaciers, snow and polar ice sheets. With Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets already melting about six times faster than in the 1990s, the report argues that global temperatures should ultimately be brought back below 1C. The Guardian reports:  The report, which comes as world leaders and diplomats converge on Turkey for the 31st annual Cop climate conference, documented rapid and accelerating melting of the cryosphere and polar oceans, with damages that range from the loss of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, driving sea level rises that threaten hundreds of millions of people, to thawing permafrost, which releases more planet-heating gas. Glaciers, which are still responding to historical warming, would only preserve about 70% of their current volume over a timescale of centuries if long-term heating were brought back down to 0.8C, the report found.
Meanwhile, the ice sheets covering Greenland and Antarctica, which are melting about six times faster today than in the 1990s, would continue to lose ice even in scenarios where overshoot is brief and temperature rise returns to 1.5C, the report found. The scientists said a safe, long-term temperature limit for polar ice sheets lies much closer to 1.0C of global heating, and possibly even lower. "Snow and ice respond rapidly to every fraction of a degree of warming," said [James Kirkham, a glaciologist at ICCI and the lead author of the report. "But most of these systems will take centuries or millennia to recover after overshoot, especially if tipping points are crossed that cause changes to become essentially irreversible."
Last month, a UNEP report found the world must cut emissions by 18% by 2030 and by 45% by 2035 to have a good chance of keeping temperatures from rising 1.7C above preindustrial levels. It found there were "no good outcomes" of remaining above 1.5C. The cryosphere report found that current policies, which will result in 2.8C of global heating, would reduce the mass of glacier ice to below 10% in the Rockies, Alps, Iceland and Scandinavia. If warming was limited to 1.5C, about 20-35% of the mass would remain. In the Hindu Kush Himalayas, where glaciers are a source of water for nearly a quarter of humanity, current policies will leave just 41% of the ice mass. If warming was limited to 1.5C, 83% would remain.

articles.title: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
articles.body:
With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.
The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
What started as a test to understand how sun exposure was aging my skin took a turn that I wasn’t expecting.
Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem, from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both.
This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside.
I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others.
The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck.
The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight.
There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score.
The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score.
The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking.
My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too.
The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun.
That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade.
I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary.
At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.
Photography by Sheena Vasani / The Verge

articles.title: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits. AI Frontiers Group Declared Finished
articles.body:
John Langford, a partner researcher manager at Microsoft Research New York, has left Microsoft.
He declared the AI Frontiers group over, according to Digg, which summarised a post on his blog, Machine Learning (Theory). Langford announced the post on social media on Nov. 6.
The group had about 50 people. It was moved out of Microsoft Research and into Microsoft AI in early September.
Langford wrote that he found places for his team members as well as he could before leaving, Digg reported.
His account does not detail the group's formal status or where remaining staff were assigned.
What AI Frontiers Built
Langford wrote that he and colleagues created AI Frontiers inside Microsoft Research in 2023. They wanted more organized research after the release of ChatGPT.
Much of the group's work centred on making AI agents function reliably.
Projects he named include Autogen, a framework for coordinating agents. Another is Fara, an agent that operates a computer to carry out tasks.
Shunyatax also described some researchers in the group as exploring ways to improve models without simply making them larger.
Scaling Versus Research
Langford described the leadership philosophy in Microsoft AI as focused on scaling rather than research, Digg reported. He said the environment focused mainly on getting, making and refining data.
He conceded the business logic. In his assessment, returns to scale are more predictable than returns to research. Still, he called a scaling-only approach misdirected and unenjoyable, Digg reported.
Those are his judgments. They concern the unit his group joined, not company-wide policy.
Shunyatax reported that Langford's position was not that scaling should stop. It said he argued scaling and fundamental research should run side by side.
No Route to Use
Langford wrote that he could not get innovations used, or even seriously considered, while in Microsoft AI. A return to Microsoft Research held little appeal.
He doubted research could reach use from there either.
Langford wrote, in a post Digg summarised, that he is not comfortable being at a company where his research has no path to real use.
He added that there will be no internships with the group in the coming year. He wished well to the colleagues he is leaving behind, according to Digg.
His profile on the research platform alphaxiv lists him as a founding member of Microsoft Research New York. It also names him a co-creator of the Vowpal Wabbit machine-learning library.
A 2023 Test of Time Award at The Web Conference recognised his contextual-bandit paper on personalised news recommendation. The paper describes algorithms that learn which article to show a reader.
Other Microsoft Departures
Shunyatax placed the AI Frontiers news alongside other senior changes at Microsoft.
It cited the planned departure of former LinkedIn chief executive Ryan Roslansky from his later responsibilities over the Office and Teams divisions.
It also cited the move of former AI platform head Eric Boyd to Anthropic.
The link is unproven. Shunyatax said the material does not establish that those changes stemmed from disagreements over research strategy, or that they are linked to Langford's exit.
