Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.
Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.
We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.
The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.
Building for agent scale
We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:
- Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few.
- Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis.
Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.
We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.
We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:
- Accept thousands of writes per second.
- Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this:
  - Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly.
  - Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails.
- Minimize commit latency. An agent waits on each push before it moves to its next step.
- Record changes in order for each reference with the ability to quickly linearize across references. A virtual replica that falls behind needs to catch up by downloading only the data it needs to serve the incoming request.
- Keep reads cheap when nothing has changed, which is the common case given the read-to-write ratio.
- Let each component scale independently.
On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.
Introducing “Project Rubicon”
In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.
Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.
Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.
Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.
When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.
Durable state lives in two places:
- Git objects, in the form of packs and auxiliary read acceleration data, live in Azure Blob Storage.
- References and the list of packs that make up the repository (the pack manifest) live in a separate replicated log service we call Ref-CAS (for “Reference Compare-and-Swap”).
Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:
- Write: a virtual replica indexes the incoming pack and uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one transaction to Ref-CAS that lists the pack in the manifest and updates the references. Later, a compaction node merges that pack with others to keep reads fast.
- Read: a virtual replica checks its reference version with Ref-CAS, pulls the packs it needs from Blob Storage into its cache, and serves the read from there.
There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.
Minimizing coordination: mutating reference state at high throughput
Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:
- Packs and indexes written by pushes, compaction, and garbage collection.
- Various read accelerators (like multi-pack indexes, reachability bitmaps, and some custom formats) that our maintenance process builds from those packs.
- Records that let compaction and garbage collection resume or audit their work, along with the leases that compaction nodes use to claim work.
- Cached responses for frequently repeated fetches.
- Checkpoints for the reference state of the repository, though not the authoritative state used to serve requests.
Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.
References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.
Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.
Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:
Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.
Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log’s replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don’t contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.
Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository’s version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.
Unlike the consensus group in our legacy architecture, Ref-CAS never holds or validates object data. It only stores pointers to it. A virtual replica uploads a push’s pack to Blob Storage before it commits the reference transaction. A reference only ever points at objects that are already durable.
These approaches allow us to transact reference state alone in the tens of thousands of operations per second, and provide a baseline for additional annotations on the replication log that help reads decide what to download for a given request.
But supporting thousands of writes per second on a single repository creates a second-order problem: maintaining the performance of reads and writes. For that, we needed a different approach to compaction.
Decoupling storage from compute: compaction at thousands of writes per second
Every push adds a pack to Blob Storage. Git can serve a repository from many packs, but each additional pack makes lookups slightly more expensive, so the pack count can’t grow without bound. In our legacy architecture, compaction runs on the same replicas that serve traffic, and it has to run on every replica. In the new architecture, it runs entirely in the background on separate nodes, directly against durable storage, using the Ref-CAS service to notify virtual replicas of the evolving state.
Compaction nodes each claim ownership over a subset of the repository’s data via a lease, which allows us to scale compaction horizontally. Here’s how one compaction node works through a single shard of a repository’s packs:
The node first takes a lease on the shard in Blob Storage, so only one node compacts a shard at a time. Meanwhile, virtual replicas keep uploading packs and listing them in the pack manifest. The node reads the manifest to find new packs and collects them into an open segment, which is effectively a holding ground for data about to be compacted. When the segment reaches a defined limit based on pack count, size, or age, it seals the segment so it accepts no new packs, then combines its packs into fewer, larger ones. While compaction happens, the next segment for the shard can begin capturing its input packs. Before anything is published, the node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects as the inputs. It then uploads the new packs and adds them to the manifest. A second transaction removes the inputs from the manifest, and cleanup deletes them later.
To scale out, this process runs independently for many shards at once. Each pack’s hash maps to a shard, so adding shards and nodes adds compaction throughput. A compacted pack that’s still under the size limit goes back into a shard by its own hash and merges again, so packs grow in tiers until they reach the limit. The net result is an effectively flat pack count while pushes climb:
Compaction merges packs, but it keeps every object. Garbage collection is the step that removes objects nothing references anymore, like the ones left behind by deleted branches and force-pushes. In our new architecture, garbage collection works very similarly to compaction by using dedicated workers to handle the compute-heavy portion. It also has a few special behaviors for safely removing data, which are worthy of their own discussion.
Using these approaches, we’ve been able to consistently demonstrate a flat latency curve as writes climb, and we have other planned optimizations to make the compaction and garbage collection processes themselves more performant.
What comes next
The two principles we started with let each part of this architecture scale on its own. We scale reads and writes by adding virtual replicas. Ref-CAS orders each reference independently instead of the whole repository. We scale maintenance by adding compaction nodes. Our goal is for every repository, from one developer’s side project to the busiest monorepo, to run on the same architecture with no special handling for the busy ones. Repositories don’t stay small. A side project can pick up a fleet of agents overnight, and it shouldn’t need a migration or special handling from us to keep up. One architecture also means every improvement we make reaches every repository at once.
This foundation lets us do a lot more. We’re focused on three areas next: scaling the architecture beyond what we can predict we’ll need today, making agents more efficient at the work they do on GitHub, and evolving Git itself for agentic development.
Improving the architecture
We have plans to take this architecture further. Each of these improvements lets a repository handle more activity while reducing the work behind each request:
- Read only what’s needed. Fetch a single object from Blob Storage instead of the whole pack that holds it.
- Organize packs by type. Group commits, trees, and blobs into their own packs. Many requests then touch less data.
- Partial replicas. Serve requests without every pack on local disk.
- Materialized views. Keep repository data in ready-to-use forms, like prepared archives, a near-live shallow copy of the default branch, and agent session context stored alongside each commit.
- Global replicas. Place replicas in any region, close to the workloads that use them. Reads stay within bounded staleness of the latest write.
- Scale to zero. Grow and shrink the fleet with the repositories that are actually active.
Efficient agent operations on GitHub
Scaling the infrastructure is one side of supporting agents. The other side is making each agent operation cheaper: fewer bytes to fetch, fewer round trips, and less waiting on changes. Each of these fast-follow items builds on the storage work in this post:
- Work without a clone. Many agent tasks never need a full working tree. They need a handful of files and enough context to make a change. They can read both straight from the server.
- Atomic commit API. Land a multi-file change in one operation. The whole change commits, or it’s rejected cleanly on conflict.
- Event streams. Agents and the systems around them work best with real-time information. A generic event stream lets them subscribe to changes and react as they happen.
Improving Git for agents
We also have work to do in Git itself. GitHub has been a longtime contributor to the Git project, and we’re not stopping now. A few examples of the work we’re excited to continue:
- Lightweight clones. Partial clone, shallow clone, and sparse checkout each let an agent fetch less. Each one has gaps. They don’t always work well together, either. We want to improve each piece and make them fit.
- Remove hidden scaling costs. Git still has code paths that slow down much faster than the repository grows. Recent releases fixed several of them, but we expect to find more.
- Faster history walks. Metadata like the commit-graph can answer merge-base and reachability questions without walking every commit. That matters most when an agent’s API call turns into Git work on the server.
- Avoid common gotchas. Agents make the same mistakes developers do. Git can catch more of the common ones and warn before they cause damage.
Agents have changed how software gets built. GitHub and Git are changing with it. We’re excited to take this new architecture across the starting line. It’s available in a limited private preview now, with a broader rollout early next year. We can’t wait to see what teams build when the number of agents working on a repository is limited by their ideas. We’ll keep evolving Git and GitHub alongside our customers and the Git community.

articles.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
articles.body:
Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.
Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.
That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.
The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development.
But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.
Here are some of the biggest takeaways.
AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development
One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.
Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.
For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”
Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps
Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.
Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.
Anthropic is keeping key information secret
Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.
And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.
METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”
METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.
In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.
“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”
McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.
Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected
The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.
For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.
The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.
Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.
On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”
Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety
Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month.
Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”
Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.
The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.”
Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs
Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.”
For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.
Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.
And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

articles.title: Ultima and Wing Commander Remasters
articles.body:
Many people are not big fans of game publisher EA right now for good reason, but for those who remember a better time in the 1990s, there’s a little good news. Twenty-five classic games from that EA era have been lightly remastered and updated, then placed for sale on Steam and GOG, including several Wing Commander games and nearly the entire Ultima series.
Below is the full list of remastered or re-released games:
- Road Rash: 30th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander: 35th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander II: Vengeance of the Kilrathi: 35th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger: 30th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander IV: The Price of Freedom: 30th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander Prophecy: 30th Anniversary Edition
- Privateer 2: The Darkening: 30th Anniversary Edition
- Wing Commander: Privateer
- Wing Commander: Academy
- Wing Commander: Armada
- Strike Commander
- Theme Hospital
- Crusader: No Remorse
- Crusader: No Regret
- Ultima I: The First Age of Darkness
- Ultima II: The Revenge of the Enchantress
- Ultima III: Exodus
- Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar
- Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny
- Ultima VI: The False Prophet
- Ultima VII: The Complete Edition
- Ultima VIII: Gold Edition
- Ultima IX: Ascension
- Ultima Underworld I
- Ultima Underworld II
The story behind seven remasters
In a lengthy blog post published this week, Jim Vessella, a senior producer at EA, described the efforts that went into remastering Wing Commander I-IV and Prophecy, Privateer 2, and Road Rash.
It’s a long, detailed story that’s worth reading yourself, but here’s a top-level summary. After working on the mostly widely acclaimed Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection in 2019, Vessella writes that he learned about and visited a room at EA’s Redwood Shores campus that contained a large archive of poorly labeled or sorted physical media from ages past.
In his free time, and with the help of others, he began cataloging this archive and discovered, among other things, that it contained virtually the entirety of the original masters of Wing Commander III and Wing Commander IV‘s full-motion-video cutscenes.
The story that ensues involves building a small team of contractors, poring through the footage 17 hours a day on swing shifts to label and digitize it, and then coordinating with several key community members—particularly Matt Wells, who has made community enhancement patches for some of the Wing Commander games—to put together remasters of those games.

articles.title: Asahi Linux Progress Linux 7.3
articles.body:
Progress Report: Linux 7.3
Well here we are again. Linux 7.3 is out and it’s been an eventful few months, so let’s get stuck in to another Asahi Linux progress report!
Upstreaming continues
As always, upstreaming work continues to progress. Aside from the usual patches for low-level SoC blocks, two major drivers made it on to the list this cycle: macaudio and avd. Getting macaudio ready for submission has been a challenge. The audio subsystem on Apple Silicon devices is rather special, and required quite a number of core ALSA changes to properly support it. Apple also uses special variants of speaker and headset amplifiers that were already supported upstream, and these drivers also needed some pretty significant modifications. We have previously discussed a lot of this work at length, and we are finally in a position where we can submit the main driver for review. The driver and Devicetree changes represent a hefty chunk of our total patchset, about 3100 lines.
AVD is a whole different beast. The AVD driver has spent barely 3 months in our downstream tree and is already on the list. We are unsure if Google intends to generalise this approach and upstream it, or if this is going to stay an Android-only patchset. As such, we do not want to ship this in our downstream tree and have folks become reliant on it when there is this level of uncertainty.
It also requires userspace integration. P3S works by checking the binary metadata for its sections’ page alignments. This works for Google’s use case, as P3S is intended as a fallback mechanism for applications aligned to 4 KiB pages. It is not worth spending the effort on implementing this until we have some certainty around what Google intends to do with this patchset.

Our IRC channels and Matrix rooms are safe spaces, open to anyone with even a passing interest in Asahi Linux or hacking on Apple Silicon.
We do all of this because we firmly believe in Free and Open Source Software, not just as a means to an end but as the end in and of itself. The modern digital world is only possible because of the Free Software movement, and it is more important now than it ever has been that we do all we can to protect the Free Software ecosystem and uphold the ideals upon which it is built.
It may surprise some to learn that WINE was originally made available under the MIT licence. Unfortunately, this is no longer viable. The malicious practices of the 90s and 2000s have reared their ugly heads once again, this time driven in large part by both the insatiable appetite of frontier AI labs for high-quality training data, and militant animosity toward the Free Software community.

The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors.
As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it.
Until next time!
As always, we would like to sincerely thank our supporters on OpenCollective and GitHub Sponsors. It is only through your generous backing that we are able to dedicate the time and resources to continuing our work reverse engineering the platform and bringing to it a world-class, polished, and battle-tested Linux desktop experience. You mean the world to us.

The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors.
As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it.
Until next time!
As always, we would like to sincerely thank our supporters on OpenCollective and GitHub Sponsors. It is only through your generous backing that we are able to dedicate the time and resources to continuing our work reverse engineering the platform and bringing to it a world-class, polished, and battle-tested Linux desktop experience. You mean the world to us.

articles.title: Google has acquired Crusoe's data center site in southeast Wyoming
articles.body:
Crusoe Announces Wyoming Data Center Campus Update
Google has acquired Crusoe’s data center site in southeast Wyoming, completing Crusoe’s pre-development work on site selection, governmental approvals, and a hybrid power strategy developed with Tallgrass Energy.
DENVER — November 6, 2026 — Crusoe, the AI factory company, today announced its site in southeast Wyoming has been acquired by Google. The transaction marks the completion of Crusoe's engagement in pre-development work on the Wyoming project – which included data center site selection, governmental approvals, and power strategy.
"Crusoe’s pre-construction efforts – origination, entitlement, and de-risking – have set up the Wyoming project for construction and eventual operation,” said Chase Lochmiller, Co-founder and CEO of Crusoe. “Crusoe is in the business of activating gigawatts for intelligence. With more than 6 GW contracted and over 40 GW in our pipeline, we are eager to steward the development and energization of the foundational infrastructure of AI.”
Crusoe and Tallgrass Energy initiated the Wyoming campus through the joint development of power and data center infrastructure. This parallel process required simultaneous coordination across energy systems design, data center engineering, site development, and hyperscaler engagement. The innovative hybrid power strategy developed for the campus exemplifies Crusoe’s integrated approach to digital infrastructure, combining fuel cells, grid power, and natural gas turbines with a long-term roadmap for carbon capture via Tallgrass’s regional CO2 sequestration hub.
Crusoe recently announced it is the developer of Google’s data center campus under construction in Armstrong County outside of Amarillo.
About Crusoe
As the AI factory company, Crusoe is on a mission to accelerate the abundance of energy and intelligence. The company provides a reliable, scalable, cost-effective, energy-first solution for AI infrastructure. By harnessing large-scale energy sources, building AI-optimized data centers, and delivering a powerful AI cloud platform, Crusoe empowers its customers and partners to build the future faster. For more information, visit crusoe.ai.
Media Contact
media@crusoe.ai

articles.title: Scientists Find Rare Meteorite From Mars With Signs of Ancient Water
articles.body:
Scientists Find Rare Meteorite From Mars With Signs of Ancient Water (msn.com)
			
		 	
				"I didn't think a rock like this existed on Earth," a geologist at the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Texas told the Washington Post.  It looks like a polished rock, dark brown with a clay-colored stripe — but it's actually one of the oldest Mars meteorites ever found, blasted by an impact from the surface of Mars billions of years ago:
Technically speaking it's a collection of eight rock fragments, the largest of which is about the size of a fist. Nearly two pounds of the meteorite was discovered in the Sahara in Mali in 2022, and most is now held by a museum in Maine. Within two years, an initial examination determined the meteorite hailed from Mars; scientists are now finally digging deeper, with stunning results. 
It offers  records of "interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water," says Lee Saper, co-author of a new paper recently published in Science.  "It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, the lead author of a new paper published in Science. "One of the paper's reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars." 
Its mix of minerals "tells a story about how the planet's crust formed from cooling magma before it was eventually altered by subsurface water," NASA's JPL says in an announcement.
The Washington Post reports:
The story begins 4.1 billion years ago, when crystals of a mineral called zircon probably solidified out of molten magma on Mars. "That was a game changer," [said Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California], since scientists can date zircon very precisely, and it has been rare in other Mars meteorites.  The date immediately put the Teghaza meteorite on special footing, alongside only two other Mars rocks known to have formed by 4 billion years ago... 
Perhaps most intriguingly, the researchers also saw signs that the rock had been exposed to water during its evolution, a find detailed in work published this summer in Science Advances.

articles.title: A Third Major US Offshore Wind Farm Is Now Fully Operational
articles.body:
A Third Major US Offshore Wind Farm Is Now Fully Operational (canarymedia.com) 5
			
		 	
				Despite the Trump administration's efforts to halt development on a $6.2 billion wind farm, it's now "completely up and running," reports the nonprofit energy news site Canary Media, delivering enough electricity to power the equivalent over 350,000 homes:
On Thursday, the Danish energy giant Ørsted said its 704-megawatt wind farm near Connecticut and Rhode Island began "generating up to its full capacity" in October. Revolution Wind began producing smaller amounts of power in the spring, and the company installed the last of 65 turbines in September.    The project is the third U.S. utility-scale offshore wind farm to reach full commercial operations, after South Fork Wind near New York and Vineyard Wind near Massachusetts.  
Before the start of Trump's second term, BloombergNEF projected America would build 39 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2035 the article points out, but "Now, it expects just 5.9 GW to come online — an amount that reflects the handful of projects that were already completed or under construction at the start of last year."
Despite the diminished pipeline, the carbon-free energy source is still expected to help keep household utility bills in check across the U.S. Northeast, experts say. Revolution Wind and the country's other completed projects have already played a key role in reducing grid stress during extreme weather events this year...
Ørsted hit its power milestone despite being forced to halt construction twice last year.  In August 2025, the Interior Department issued a stop-work order for Revolution Wind, due to unspecified national security threats. That order was tossed out by a federal judge one month later. But in late December, the administration issued new stop-work orders to all five offshore wind projects then under construction. Judges struck those orders down one by one — but not before developers had lost huge sums of money and nearly missed key project deadlines...
Meanwhile, Ørsted said it's making progress on another offshore wind development, Sunrise Wind. The developer on Thursday said it has finished installing all of the wind-turbine foundations for the 924-MW project off the coast of Long Island, New York. That installation is expected to be fully operational in the second half of next year.

articles.title: Every Windows 11 app should kill Electron, and Discord just showed why
articles.body:
Discord’s new Rust client had its friends list loaded before the current Electron app could get past its loading screen, in a 15-second clip that we found on the X account of Discord co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy. The video had 2.3 million views at the time of writing, and Discord employees have confirmed that both apps were launched from a cold start.
Vishnevskiy also revealed that the 290.2MB RAM usage on the Task Manager of the new client, which shows up as Discord Phoenix, came with two accounts signed in at once, which justifies the already efficient RAM usage.
Discord’s Rust client opens before the Electron app finishes loading
“The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time,” Vishnevskiy wrote on X, and Discord’s official account also shared the clip with the current client on the left and the Rust rebuild on the right.
We went through the video frame by frame. What’s impressive is that the current client is opened first and shows a blank dark window for about three seconds, followed by a tip that reads “In the ancient days, Discord started as a browser-only app.” Funnily enough, the Electron app still carries a browser engine today.
The new client is double-clicked roughly a second and a half later, yet its window fades in within a second. When the old app reaches its interface, about five seconds after launch, the Rust version already has the friends list loaded, while the Electron client briefly says “There are no friends online at this time.”
Of course, people on X asked if the new app simply popped out of the system tray. “Both are cold starts, it’s really that fast. We’ve been using it internally now for a while and the first time I tried it I thought I’d forgot to close it when I opened it fresh,” replied Coral, who leads audio and video at Discord.
Travis, who works on socials and community at Discord and filmed the clip, added that a tray launch would mean “the friends list would have already been loaded!” Vishnevskiy thanked him for “finding these janky old laptops,” which are ThinkPads with a Copilot key, so 2024 or newer, which I wouldn’t dare call janky or old. They’re beautiful machines!
The new Discord app skips the “Starting” screen and updates in the background
As you’d already know, the current app usually checks for updates and shows a “Starting” screen when you open it, which one person on X said “takes like 5-10s every time.” Asked why the new client skips it, coral said, “It bootstraps so fast + is a new architecture so we don’t need that modal at all. We auto-update in the background.”
Discord isn’t handing updates to the Microsoft Store or Windows’ Update Orchestration Platform either, as Coral said “We do not at this moment” when asked.
Discord’s Rust client uses about 70% less RAM with two accounts signed in
When one reply called 290MB “still vile” for a chat app, Vishnevskiy said, “Those 4k avatar decorations gotta render somewhere ;) but joking aside this client is actually running 2 accounts concurrently which is supported in new client.”
Today’s Account Switcher lets you add up to five accounts and swap between them. Asked if the new client could keep work and personal accounts running “without needing to tear down the client in between,” Vishnevskiy replied “Yup.” Again, impressive and exciting.
For comparison, a Discord employee said in December 2025 that normal usage is under 1GB, while the company tested auto-restarting the app at 4GB. So, 290.2MB is about 70% below the 1GB mark, and on our PCs, the Electron app usually idles at 1-2GB. To be clear, it’s a snapshot from an early build, and Discord hasn’t published a like-for-like benchmark of both clients, but we’ll be doing that test when we get hands-on with the Rust version.
Discord did try to fix Electron from the inside. Its September patch notes say the Electron 42 upgrade cut median CPU usage by about 17%, but “at the cost of a smaller regression to p50 memory usage (~4%).” Even the Game Mode toggle it tested later doesn’t mention RAM.
Discord is replacing Electron with GPUI, not Tauri
Electron inherits its multi-process architecture from Chromium, so every Electron app comes with its own browser engine, with a main process and a renderer process for each window. Tauri, which many guessed Discord would pick, uses Rust for app logic but builds the interface in HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside the system’s webview, which is WebView2 on Windows.
Discord went with GPUI, “A fast, hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework for Rust” from the makers of the Zed code editor. GPUI draws the interface on the GPU without any HTML, and Rust, which Discord has used since 2018, manages memory without a garbage collector.
Why not WinUI, you ask? (At least, I thought of it). Discord hasn’t mentioned it, and it was unlikely to, as Microsoft’s native framework only runs on Windows, while GPUI already powers Zed on Windows, macOS and Linux. Discord has its own patches on top of GPUI, and Vishnevskiy said “we will see what we can upstream if relevant to the community.”
Web tech stays where it makes sense, as YouTube embeds and Activities will use the system webview. “We use the native webview similar to Tauri,” Vishnevskiy said about Activities.
Discord’s mobile apps drop React Native, and the web app moves to WebAssembly
Phones keep native interfaces but will share app code with desktop through Rust. On React Native, Vishnevskiy explained, “Since the beginning the iOS app started as React native, Android was ported to React Native couple years ago to achieve parity as it was always lagging in features.”
The browser version will keep rendering HTML, but “logic will be WASM instead of JS.” WebAssembly (WASM) lets code written in languages like Rust run inside a browser, so the web app can share the Rust code too. As for the look, whether you like it or not, “The app looks and works identically to the current one,” Vishnevskiy said.
Discord’s Rust client goes into private testing soon
If you can’t to try it out, Discord marketing director Ryan K. Rigney said, “Going into private testing soon. Gonna take our time to make sure it’s stable and secure first. Won’t be long, tho.” I would rather wait for them to iron out any bugs.
Mark Smith, Discord’s VP of Engineering, added that “accessibility and security are just as important to us as performance,” and Coral confirmed the new client keeps your login token in the system keyring, which is Credential Manager on Windows 10 and 11.
Of course, Discord is not just doing all this work for Windows. When asked if it works on Linux, Rigney replied, “Yes,” and Coral said, “a lot of people run Mac internally!” Discord hasn’t announced a public release date yet.
Discord just made WhatsApp and Teams look worse on Windows 11
Electron made it easier for Discord to ship one desktop app on Windows, macOS, and Linux for a decade. But Discord has now shown that a chat app with millions of users can drop the bundled browser without a redesign.
As for the owners of the biggest messaging platforms for regular users and enterprises, Meta and Microsoft are running out of excuses. WhatsApp went from a native app that idled under 100MB to a WebView2 wrapper using up to 1.2GB, and I uninstalled it. Microsoft Teams also uses WebView2, took up 963MB doing nothing in our tests, and it doesn’t look like Redmond cares enough to go native, despite pushing WinUI.
Ironically, AI got us here. Data centers soaked up DRAM supply, prices shot up, and Windows chief Pavan Davuluri now says “memory is top of mind for us right now in the industry” as Microsoft trims Windows 11’s RAM usage. Apps that kept asking for more RAM are finally going on a diet, and we’ve come full circle.
Are you waiting to try the Rust-based Discord when it rolls out?

articles.title: Outbound SIP calling is now available to all organizations
articles.body:
Choose your API to see its connection steps and session events.
Connect incoming and outgoing phone calls to GPT-Live through a SIP trunk. Your provider exchanges call audio with OpenAI, while your backend handles session configuration, call controls, and business logic. SIP signaling uses TLS, and GPT-Live requires SRTP for call audio.
- Handle an inbound call: receive an incoming-call webhook, then accept or reject the call.
- Place an outbound call: create a session to dial a phone number through your provider. No incoming-call webhook or accept request is needed.
Use a sideband connection when your backend needs to receive session events or send commands. It attaches to the existing conversation while SIP carries the audio. Assign one handler to each action so that duplicate webhook deliveries or events observed on multiple connections don’t execute tools twice.
Handle an inbound call
Route incoming phone calls from your SIP provider to your OpenAI project. Your backend receives a webhook and decides whether to accept each call.
Configure your phone number and trunk
Use a SIP trunking provider, such as Twilio, to connect a phone number to GPT-Live. After purchasing a number from your provider:
- Open your project in OpenAI settings. Under Webhooks, create a webhook endpoint subscribed to live.transport.incoming.
- Find your project ID under General. It starts with proj_; use the same project that owns the webhook.
- Point your provider’s SIP trunk at sip:$PROJECT_ID@sip.api.openai.com;transport=tls. For European data residency, use sip:$PROJECT_ID@sip-eu.api.openai.com;transport=tls instead.
Confirm that GPT-Live SIP support is enabled for your project and that your provider’s SIP trunk is routed to that project before using this flow.
Receive the incoming call
When OpenAI receives a call for your project, it sends a live.transport.incoming event to your webhook endpoint. Verify the webhook signature and deduplicate deliveries, then accept or reject the call.
The webhook identifies a SIP call with data.type: "sip" and provides data.session_id. Use that session ID unchanged for every Live call action. Treat data.sip_headers as untrusted caller metadata, not authorization.
For example, the webhook body contains:
{
  "object": "event",
  "id": "evt_abc123",
  "type": "live.transport.incoming",
  "created_at": 1750287018,
  "data": {
    "type": "sip",
    "session_id": "live_123",
    "sip_headers": [
      { "name": "From", "value": "sip:+14155550123@sip.example.com" },
      { "name": "To", "value": "sip:+18005550100@sip.example.com" },
      { "name": "Call-ID", "value": "call-123@example.com" }
    ]
  }
}
The created_at field is a Unix timestamp in seconds. Delivery headers include webhook-id for deduplication, webhook-timestamp for the delivery attempt, and webhook-signature for signature verification. See webhook verification examples for server-side handlers.
Existing integrations may still receive the deprecated live.call.incoming event, which has no data.type. During migration, handle both names and retain the old subscription until legacy deliveries and retries have drained. The same pending call can also emit a Realtime webhook; assign one handler to the accept/reject decision rather than accepting through both APIs.
Accept or reject the call
Apply your application’s authorization and routing rules. To accept the call, send an authenticated POST /v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/accept request with a top-level session object:
{
  "session": {
    "type": "live",
    "model": "gpt-live-1",
    "instructions": "You are answering an inbound support call.",
    "audio": { "output": { "voice": "marin" } },
    "delegation": { "type": "client" }
  }
}
Use Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY from your trusted backend for call-control requests. Choose the voice and delegation mode at acceptance. SIP negotiates the audio format, so omit audio.format. The example selects client delegation; your backend must handle delegated work. See Delegation and tools for client and Responses configurations.
A successful acceptance returns 200 OK with an empty body after session initialization. Handle HTTP errors before treating the call as accepted.
To reject the call, send POST /v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/reject with a SIP status, such as { "status_code": 486 } for busy. The status must be an integer from 300 through 699. The first accept or reject decision wins; a later competing decision returns decision_already_made.
Attach your backend
After acceptance, connect a sideband WebSocket at wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/attach. Use the accepted session ID and the same project authentication and connection headers. Do not send session.start again.
SIP carries the call audio. Use the sideband for transcripts, delegation, tools, commands, and reflected audio. Choose one owner for each side effect, even if multiple connections observe an event.
Once connected, use the active call controls to send keypad tones, transfer the call, or hang up.
Place an outbound call
Call a phone number through your SIP provider with Create session. Your provider handles the phone network connection while GPT-Live carries the conversation.
Outbound SIP calling is available to all organizations through the Live API, not the Realtime API call-creation endpoint.
Configure your trunk
Use a trunk that supports TLS signaling and SDES-SRTP media. Enable SRTP in your provider’s settings before placing a call.
Supply the trunk configuration with each request:
The provider endpoint must use sips: for TLS signaling. Don’t include credentials, paths, URI headers, or other URI parameters in the URL. Local hostnames and literal private or local IP addresses are rejected. Keep your OpenAI API key and SIP credentials on your server.
Create the session
Send POST /v1/live/sessions with your session configuration and transport.type: "sip". Choose the voice and delegation mode when creating the session. Omit audio.format because SIP negotiates the audio format.
This example uses curl and jq. Set OPENAI_API_KEY, SIP_USERNAME, and SIP_PASSWORD in your server environment, and replace the example provider endpoint and phone numbers with your own values. The example selects client delegation; your backend must handle delegated work.
jq -n \
  --arg username "$SIP_USERNAME" \
  --arg password "$SIP_PASSWORD" \
  '{
    "session": {
      "model": "gpt-live-1",
      "instructions": "Help the user schedule an appointment.",
      "audio": { "output": { "voice": "marin" } },
      "delegation": { "type": "client" }
    },
    "transport": {
      "type": "sip",
      "destination": "+14155550123",
      "trunk": {
        "provider_url": "sips:sip.example.com:5061",
        "auth": {
          "type": "digest",
          "username": $username,
          "password": $password
        },
        "caller_number": "+14155550100"
      }
    }
  }' | curl https://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    --data-binary @-
The request returns 200 OK after the session initializes:
{
  "session": { "id": "live_123" },
  "transport": { "type": "sip" }
}
This response doesn’t mean the call has been answered. It contains no SDP or trunk credentials. Preserve session.id unchanged for the sideband connection and call controls. You don’t need an incoming-call webhook or an accept request for an outbound call.
Monitor and end the call
Attach your backend to wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/attach using your OpenAI API key. Don’t send session.start again. The sideband connection carries conversation events, delegated work, and call progress while SIP carries the audio.
Each call-progress event includes event_id and session_id. Attach immediately after creation: the sideband only replays events from the preceding 3 seconds, so a later attachment can miss earlier call progress. Replayed events retain their original event IDs. Deduplicate events by event_id.
Once connected, use the active call controls to send keypad tones, transfer the call, or hang up. Keep the sideband open for session.closed and final usage as described in Usage and graceful close.
Handle limits and errors
Ringing is limited to 3 minutes, and a connected call is limited to 2 hours. These limits aren’t configurable in the creation request.
Invalid session configuration is returned on the creation request. Transport setup failures can return 502, and initialization timeouts return 504. After creation succeeds, monitor transport.failed for asynchronous setup failures.
Manage an active call
These controls apply to both inbound and outbound SIP calls.
Send and receive keypad events
The sideband receives transport.dtmf.received when the caller presses a key. To send a DTMF tone to the SIP trunk, send a transport.dtmf.send client event over the sideband WebSocket. After the tone is successfully sent, the sideband receives transport.dtmf.sent.
If you supply an event_id, the notification includes it as client_event_id; failures return an error event with error.client_event_id.
Transfer or end the call
To transfer the call, send POST /v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/refer with { "target_uri": "sip:agent@example.com" } for your destination. To hang up, send POST /v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/hangup with no request body. Both return 200 OK with an empty body on success.
The transfer target becomes the SIP Refer-To header and can be a telephone URI such as tel:+14155550123 or a SIP URI such as sip:agent@example.com. Your provider handles the remaining transfer flow.
Keep the sideband open until session.closed supplies final usage. See Usage and graceful close for usage reporting and close reasons.
SIP network requirements
GPT-Live SIP calls use separate network paths for signaling and media. Configure your network to allow both:
- SIP signaling: sip.api.openai.com and sip-eu.api.openai.com are GeoIP-routed endpoints. Allow outbound TCP/TLS traffic to the addresses returned by DNS on port 5061.
- SRTP media: The API specifies a separate media IP address and UDP port in the negotiated SDP. Allow bidirectional SRTP traffic over UDP to and from the following CIDRs:
  - 13.79.45.80/28
  - 23.98.140.64/28
  - 40.67.149.176/28
  - 40.83.204.240/28
Next steps with GPT-Live
- Prompting guide: write instructions for your voice agent.
- Webhooks and server-side controls: manage a session from your backend.
- Delegation and tools: connect speech to your reasoning and tool backend.
- Managing sessions: handle transcripts, session state, and close.
- Latency and cost: understand latency and usage.
- GPT-Live partner integrations: find provider-specific setup guides and examples.
SIP is a protocol used to make phone calls over the internet. With SIP and the Realtime API you can direct incoming phone calls to the API.
Overview
If you want to connect a phone number to the Realtime API, use a SIP trunking provider (e.g., Twilio). This is a service that converts your phone call to IP traffic. After you purchase a phone number from your SIP trunking provider, follow the instructions below.
Start by creating a webhook for incoming calls, through your platform.openai.com settings > Project > Webhooks.
Then, point your SIP trunk at the OpenAI SIP endpoint, using the project ID
for which you configured the webhook, e.g., sip:$PROJECT_ID@sip.api.openai.com;transport=tls.
For European data residency, use sip:$PROJECT_ID@sip-eu.api.openai.com;transport=tls instead.
To find your $PROJECT_ID, visit settings > Project > General. That page will display the project ID, which
will have a proj_ prefix.
When OpenAI receives SIP traffic associated with your project,
your webhook will be fired. The event fired will be a
realtime.call.incoming event,
like the example below:
POST https://my_website.com/webhook_endpoint
user-agent: OpenAI/1.0 (+https://platform.openai.com/docs/webhooks)
content-type: application/json
webhook-id: wh_685342e6c53c8190a1be43f081506c52 # unique id for idempotency
webhook-timestamp: 1750287078 # timestamp of delivery attempt
webhook-signature: v1,K5oZfzN95Z9UVu1EsfQmfVNQhnkZ2pj9o9NDN/H/pI4= # signature to verify authenticity from OpenAI
{
  "object": "event",
  "id": "evt_685343a1381c819085d44c354e1b330e",
  "type": "realtime.call.incoming",
  "created_at": 1750287018, // Unix timestamp
  "data": {
    "call_id": "some_unique_id",
    "sip_headers": [
      { "name": "From", "value": "sip:+142555512112@sip.example.com" },
      { "name": "To", "value": "sip:+18005551212@sip.example.com" },
      { "name": "Call-ID", "value": "03782086-4ce9-44bf-8b0d-4e303d2cc590"}
    ]
  }
}
From this webhook, you can accept or reject the call, using the call_id value from the webhook.
When accepting the call, you’ll provide the needed configuration
(instructions, voice, etc) for the Realtime API session.
Once established, you can set up a WebSocket and monitor the session as usual. The APIs to
accept, reject, monitor, refer, and hangup the call are documented below.
Accept the call
Use the Accept call endpoint to
approve the inbound call and configure the realtime session that will answer it.
Send the same parameters you would send in a
create client secret
request, i.e., ensure the realtime model, voice, tools, or instructions are set before bridging the
call to the model.
curl -X POST "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls/$CALL_ID/accept" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "type": "realtime",
        "model": "gpt-realtime-2.1",
        "instructions": "You are Alex, a friendly concierge for Example Corp."
      }'
The request path must include the call_id from the
realtime.call.incoming
webhook, and every request requires the Authorization header shown above. The
endpoint returns 200 OK once the SIP leg is ringing and the realtime session
is being established.
Reject the call
Use the Reject call endpoint to
decline an invite when you do not want to handle the incoming call, (e.g., from
an unsupported country code.) Supply the call_id path parameter
and an optional SIP status_code (e.g., 486 to indicate “busy”) in the JSON
body to control the response sent back to the carrier.
curl -X POST "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls/$CALL_ID/reject" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"status_code": 486}'
If no status code is supplied the API uses 603 Decline by default. A
successful request responds with 200 OK after OpenAI delivers the SIP
response.
Monitor call events
After you accept a call, open a WebSocket connection to the same session to
stream events and issue realtime commands. Note that when connecting to an existing
call using the call_id parameter, the model argument is not used (as it has already been configured
via the accept endpoint).
WebSocket request
GET wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id={call_id}
Query parameters
Headers
- Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
The WebSocket behaves exactly like any other Realtime API connection. Send
response.create,
and other client events to control the call, and listen for server events to
track progress. See Webhooks and server-side controls
for more information.
import WebSocket from "ws";
const callId = "rtc_u1_9c6574da8b8a41a18da9308f4ad974ce";
const ws = new WebSocket(`wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id=${callId}`, {
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY}`,
  },
});
ws.on("open", () => {
  ws.send(
    JSON.stringify({
      type: "response.create",
    })
  );
});
Redirect the call
Transfer an active call using the
Refer call endpoint. Provide the
call_id as well as the target_uri that should be placed in the SIP Refer-To
header (for example tel:+14155550123 or sip:agent@example.com).
curl -X POST "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls/$CALL_ID/refer" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"target_uri": "tel:+14155550123"}'
OpenAI returns 200 OK once the REFER is relayed to your SIP provider. The
downstream system handles the rest of the call flow for the caller.
Hang up the call
End the session with the Hang up endpoint when your application should disconnect the caller. This endpoint can be used to terminate both SIP and WebRTC realtime sessions.
curl -X POST "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls/$CALL_ID/hangup" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY"
The API responds with 200 OK when it starts tearing down the call.
SIP signaling and media IP ranges
Realtime SIP calls use separate network paths for signaling and media. To ensure proper operation, configure your network to allow signaling and media traffic as described below.
SIP signaling
sip.api.openai.com and sip-eu.api.openai.com are GeoIP-routed endpoints. Your network must allow
outbound TCP/TLS traffic to the addresses returned by DNS on port 5061.
SRTP media
The API specifies a separate media IP address and UDP port in the negotiated SDP. Your network must allow bidirectional SRTP traffic over UDP to and from the following CIDRs:
- 13.79.45.80/28
- 23.98.140.64/28
- 40.67.149.176/28
- 40.83.204.240/28
Server examples
The following is an example of a realtime.call.incoming handler. It accepts the call and then logs all the events from
the Realtime API.
For the Ruby example, set the OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET
environment variables, then install the required dependencies with
gem install openai webrick async-websocket.
from flask import Flask, request, Response, jsonify, make_response
from openai import OpenAI, InvalidWebhookSignatureError
import asyncio
import json
import os
import requests
import time
import threading
import websockets
app = Flask(__name__)
client = OpenAI(webhook_secret=os.environ["OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET"])
AUTH_HEADER = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]}
call_accept = {
    "type": "realtime",
    "instructions": "You are a support agent.",
    "model": "gpt-realtime-2.1",
}
response_create = {
    "type": "response.create",
    "response": {
        "instructions": ("Say to the user 'Thank you for calling, how can I help you'")
    },
}
async def websocket_task(call_id):
    try:
        async with websockets.connect(
            "wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id=" + call_id,
            additional_headers=AUTH_HEADER,
        ) as websocket:
            await websocket.send(json.dumps(response_create))
            while True:
                response = await websocket.recv()
                print(f"Received from WebSocket: {response}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"WebSocket error: {e}")
@app.route("/", methods=["POST"])
def webhook():
    try:
        event = client.webhooks.unwrap(request.data, request.headers)
    except (InvalidWebhookSignatureError, ValueError) as e:
        print("Invalid signature", e)
        return Response("Invalid signature", status=400)
    if event.type == "realtime.call.incoming":
        requests.post(
            "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls/"
            + event.data.call_id
            + "/accept",
            headers={**AUTH_HEADER, "Content-Type": "application/json"},
            json=call_accept,
        ).raise_for_status()
        threading.Thread(
            target=lambda: asyncio.run(websocket_task(event.data.call_id)),
            daemon=True,
        ).start()
    return Response(status=200)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=8000)
Next steps
Now that you’ve connected over SIP, use the left navigation or click into these pages to start building your realtime application.
