Connect incoming and outgoing phone calls to GPT-Live through a SIP trunk. Your provider exchanges call audio with OpenAI, while your backend handles session configuration, call controls, and business logic. SIP signaling uses TLS, and GPT-Live requires SRTP for call audio.
- Handle an inbound call: receive an incoming-call webhook, then accept or reject the call.
- Place an outbound call: create a session to dial a phone number through your provider. No incoming-call webhook or accept request is needed.
Use a sideband connection when your backend needs to receive session events or send commands. It attaches to the existing conversation while SIP carries the audio. Assign one handler to each action so that duplicate webhook deliveries or events observed on multiple connections don’t execute tools twice.
Handle an inbound call
Route incoming phone calls from your SIP provider to your OpenAI project. Your backend receives a webhook and decides whether to accept each call.
Configure your phone number and trunk
Use a SIP trunking provider, such as Twilio, to connect a phone number to GPT-Live. After purchasing a number from your provider:
- Open your project in OpenAI settings. Under Webhooks, create a webhook endpoint subscribed to live.transport.incoming.
- Find your project ID under General. It starts with proj_; use the same project that owns the webhook.
- Point your provider’s SIP trunk at sip:$PROJECT_ID@sip.api.openai.com;transport=tls. For European data residency, use sip:$PROJECT_ID@sip-eu.api.openai.com;transport=tls instead.
Confirm that GPT-Live SIP support is enabled for your project and that your provider’s SIP trunk is routed to that project before using this flow.
Receive the incoming call
When OpenAI receives a call for your project, it sends a live.transport.incoming event to your webhook endpoint. Verify the webhook signature and deduplicate deliveries, then accept or reject the call.
The webhook identifies a SIP call with data.type: "sip" and provides data.session_id. Use that session ID unchanged for every Live call action. Treat data.sip_headers as untrusted caller metadata, not authorization.
For example, the webhook body contains:
{
  "object": "event",
  "id": "evt_abc123",
  "type": "live.transport.incoming",
  "created_at": 1750287018,
  "data": {
    "type": "sip",
    "session_id": "live_123",
    "sip_headers": [
      { "name": "From", "value": "sip:+14155550123@sip.example.com" },
      { "name": "To", "value": "sip:+18005550100@sip.example.com" },
      { "name": "Call-ID", "value": "call-123@example.com" }
    ]
  }
}
The created_at field is a Unix timestamp in seconds. Delivery headers include webhook-id for deduplication, webhook-timestamp for the delivery attempt, and webhook-signature for signature verification. See webhook verification examples for server-side handlers.
Existing integrations may still receive the deprecated live.call.incoming event, which has no data.type. During migration, handle both names and retain the old subscription until legacy deliveries and retries have drained. The same pending call can also emit a Realtime webhook; assign one handler to the accept/reject decision rather than accepting through both APIs.
Accept or reject the call
Apply your application’s authorization and routing rules. To accept the call, send an authenticated POST /v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/accept request with a top-level session object:
{
  "session": {
    "type": "live",
    "model": "gpt-live-1",
    "instructions": "You are answering an inbound support call.",
    "audio": { "output": { "voice": "marin" } },
    "delegation": { "type": "client" }
  }
}
Use Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY from your trusted backend for call-control requests. Choose the voice and delegation mode at acceptance. SIP negotiates the audio format, so omit audio.format. The example selects client delegation; your backend must handle delegated work. See Delegation and tools for client and Responses configurations.
A successful acceptance returns 200 OK with an empty body after session initialization. Handle HTTP errors before treating the call as accepted.
To reject the call, send POST /v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/reject with a SIP status, such as { "status_code": 486 } for busy. The status must be an integer from 300 through 699. The first accept or reject decision wins; a later competing decision returns decision_already_made.
Attach your backend
After acceptance, connect a sideband WebSocket at wss://api.openai.com/v1/live/sessions/{session_id}/attach. Use the accepted session ID and the same project authentication and connection headers. Do not send session.start again.
SIP carries the call audio. Use the sideband for transcripts, delegation, tools, commands, and reflected audio. Choose one owner for each side effect, even if multiple connections observe an event.
Once connected, use the active call controls to send keypad tones, transfer the call, or hang up.
Place an outbound call
Call a phone number through your SIP provider with Create session. Your provider handles the phone network connection while GPT-Live carries the conversation.
Outbound SIP calling is available to all organizations through the Live API, not the Realtime API call-creation endpoint.
Configure your trunk
Use a trunk that supports TLS signaling and SDES-SRTP media. Enable SRTP in your provider’s settings before placing a call.
Supply the trunk configuration with each request:
The provider endpoint must use sips: for TLS signaling. Don’t include credentials, paths, URI headers, or other URI parameters in the URL. Local hostnames and literal private or local IP addresses are rejected. Keep your OpenAI API key and SIP credentials on your server.

Send POST /v1/live/sessions with your session configuration and transport.type: "sip". Choose the voice and delegation mode when creating the session. Omit audio.format because SIP negotiates the audio format.

  --arg username "$SIP_USERNAME" \
  --arg password "$SIP_PASSWORD" \

      "delegation": { "type": "client" }

        "auth": {

          "password": $password

        "caller_number": "+14155550100"

    }

If you supply an event_id, the notification includes it as client_event_id; failures return an error event with error.client_event_id.

  - 13.79.45.80/28
  - 23.98.140.64/28
  - 40.67.149.176/28
  - 40.83.204.240/28

Query parameters
Headers
- Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
The WebSocket behaves exactly like any other Realtime API connection. Send
response.create,
and other client events to control the call, and listen for server events to
track progress. See Webhooks and server-side controls
for more information.
import WebSocket from "ws";
const callId = "rtc_u1_9c6574da8b8a41a18da9308f4ad974ce";
const ws = new WebSocket(`wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id=${callId}`, {
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY}`,
  },
});
ws.on("open", () => {
  ws.send(
    JSON.stringify({
      type: "response.create",
    })
  );
});
Redirect the call
Transfer an active call using the
Refer call endpoint. Provide the
call_id as well as the target_uri that should be placed in the SIP Refer-To
header (for example tel:+14155550123 or sip:agent@example.com).
curl -X POST "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls/$CALL_ID/refer" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"target_uri": "tel:+14155550123"}'
OpenAI returns 200 OK once the REFER is relayed to your SIP provider. The
downstream system handles the rest of the call flow for the caller.
Hang up the call
End the session with the Hang up endpoint when your application should disconnect the caller. This endpoint can be used to terminate both SIP and WebRTC realtime sessions.
curl -X POST "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls/$CALL_ID/hangup" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY"
The API responds with 200 OK when it starts tearing down the call.
SIP signaling and media IP ranges
Realtime SIP calls use separate network paths for signaling and media. To ensure proper operation, configure your network to allow signaling and media traffic as described below.
SIP signaling
sip.api.openai.com and sip-eu.api.openai.com are GeoIP-routed endpoints. Your network must allow
outbound TCP/TLS traffic to the addresses returned by DNS on port 5061.
SRTP media
The API specifies a separate media IP address and UDP port in the negotiated SDP. Your network must allow bidirectional SRTP traffic over UDP to and from the following CIDRs:
- 13.79.45.80/28
- 23.98.140.64/28
- 40.67.149.176/28
- 40.83.204.240/28
Server examples
The following is an example of a realtime.call.incoming handler. It accepts the call and then logs all the events from
the Realtime API.
For the Ruby example, set the OPENAI_API_KEY and OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET
environment variables, then install the required dependencies with
gem install openai webrick async-websocket.
from flask import Flask, request, Response, jsonify, make_response
from openai import OpenAI, InvalidWebhookSignatureError
import asyncio
import json
import os
import requests
import time
import threading
import websockets
app = Flask(__name__)
client = OpenAI(webhook_secret=os.environ["OPENAI_WEBHOOK_SECRET"])
AUTH_HEADER = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]}
call_accept = {
    "type": "realtime",
    "instructions": "You are a support agent.",
    "model": "gpt-realtime-2.1",
}
response_create = {
    "type": "response.create",
    "response": {
        "instructions": ("Say to the user 'Thank you for calling, how can I help you'")
    },
}
async def websocket_task(call_id):
    try:
        async with websockets.connect(
            "wss://api.openai.com/v1/realtime?call_id=" + call_id,
            additional_headers=AUTH_HEADER,
        ) as websocket:
            await websocket.send(json.dumps(response_create))
            while True:
                response = await websocket.recv()
                print(f"Received from WebSocket: {response}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"WebSocket error: {e}")
@app.route("/", methods=["POST"])
def webhook():
    try:
        event = client.webhooks.unwrap(request.data, request.headers)
    except (InvalidWebhookSignatureError, ValueError) as e:
        print("Invalid signature", e)
        return Response("Invalid signature", status=400)
    if event.type == "realtime.call.incoming":
        requests.post(
            "https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls/"
            + event.data.call_id
            + "/accept",
            headers={**AUTH_HEADER, "Content-Type": "application/json"},
            json=call_accept,
        ).raise_for_status()
        threading.Thread(
            target=lambda: asyncio.run(websocket_task(event.data.call_id)),
            daemon=True,
        ).start()
    return Response(status=200)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=8000)
Next steps
Now that you’ve connected over SIP, use the left navigation or click into these pages to start building your realtime application.

articles.title: As the Japanese countryside empties out, wildlife is disappearing
articles.body:
The Japanese population is in decline, but the downward trend is especially pronounced in rural areas. The loss of people might be expected to lead to a resurgence of wildlife. But paradoxically, where farms have been abandoned, wildlife is also disappearing.
Researchers say that small farms in the Japanese foothills have created mosaic landscapes with rice paddies, open pastures, and scattered woodlands that provide homes to many kinds of wildlife. Where humans cut down trees for firewood and gathered leaves for fertilizer, they made room for orchids and azaleas, Nature reports. Where farmers dug rice paddies, they made a home for rice fish and heike fireflies. Broadly speaking, many species found on farms have evolved together with humans, scientists say.
A 2025 study from Japan found that biodiversity was stable only in places where the human population was also stable. In areas where the population had declined, researchers recorded a drop in the abundance of butterflies, fireflies, frogs, birds, and native plants.
The trends in Japan mirror those in many other nations, from Spain to China, where rural areas are emptying out as people move to cities in search of work. Landscapes that were shaped by people are being taken back by nature, but often to the detriment of species that depended on human tending.
A recent study of the Lake Constance region in the European Alps found that plant diversity peaked in the medieval era, when small farms created a patchwork of fields, pastures, and forests that supported a greater array of plants than either the closed forests that came before or the industrial farms that would follow.
“The broader lesson is that, in modern conservation, the choice isn’t simply between farming and biodiversity,” said its lead author, Adam Spitzig, a PhD candidate at Stanford University. Small, diversified farms, he said, “can boost and sustain biodiversity while supporting food production.”

articles.title: Five Memorable Books About Programming
articles.body:
It's not about technology for its own sake. It's about being able to implement your ideas.
I've read the classics--Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, Paradigms of Artificial Intelligence Programming--but I'd like to highlight some of the more esoteric books which affected my thinking.
Zen of Assembly Language
Michael Abrash, 1990
I spent much of the 1980s writing 8-bit computer games (which you can read about if you like). Odd as it may seem in retrospect, considering the relative power of an 8-bit 6502 running at sub 2 MHz, I wasn't obsessed with optimizing for performance. If anything, I wanted the code to be small, a side effect of using a line-based editor and writing programs that someone would have to painstakingly type in from a magazine listing. Pages of DATA 0AFF6CA900004021... ugh.
Right when that period of my life came to a close, along came Zen of Assembly Language, by an author I had never heard of, which dissected, explained, and extended the self-taught tricks from my years as a lone assembly hacker. Even though Abrash was focused on the 8086 and not the 6502, it felt like the book was written personally to me.
This is also one of the most bizarrely delayed technical book releases I can recall. The majority of the book was about detailed optimization for the 8088 and 8086, yet it was published when the 80486 was showing up in high-end desktop PCs.
Scientific Forth
Julian Noble, 1992
Fractals, Visualization, and J
Clifford Reiter, 2000
These two books are about entirely different subjects. One is about pure scientific computation. The other is about generating images. Each uses a different, wildly non-mainstream language for the included code.
And yet these two books follow the same general approach, one I wish were more commonly used. Superficially, the authors have written introductions to particular programming languages (which is why the language name is in the title). But in reality it's more that each author has an area of deep expertise and has found a language that enables experimenting with and writing code to solve problems in that field. As such, there aren't forced examples and toy problems, but serious, non-trivial programs that show a language in actual use. Dr. Noble demonstrates how he uses Forth for hardcore matrix work and, when he realizes that RPN notation isn't ideal in all circumstances, develops a translator from infix expressions to Forth. Clifford Reiter jumps into image processing algorithms, plus veers into lighter weight diversions with titles like "R/S Analysis, the Hurst Exponent, and Sunspots."
Both books are wonderful alternatives to the usual "Learning Programing Language of the Month" texts. Sadly, Julian Noble died in 2007.
Programmers At Work
Susan Lammers, 1986
I used to soak up printed interviews with programmers and game designers (and typically game designers were programmers as well). I was enthralled by Levy's Hackers, more the game development chapter than the rest. Programmers At Work was in the same vein: philosophies, ideas, and experiences directly from an odd mix of famous and quirky programmers. But the book wasn't primarily about tech. It was about creativity. Most of the people interviewed didn't have degrees in computer science. There wasn't an emphasis on math, proving programs correct, lambda calculus--just people coming up with ideas and implementing them. And the game connection was there: Jaron Lanier talking about the psychedelic Moon Dust for the Commodore 64, Bill Budge's bold (and still unfulfilled) plan to build a "Construction Set Construction Set."
Lammers's book was the model I used when I put together Halcyon Days. I also pulled Hackers into the mix by interviewing John Harris about his dissatisfaction with Levy's presentation of him. In an odd twist of fate, Programmers at Work and Halcyon Days were packaged together on a single CD sold through the Dr. Dobb's Journal library. The pairing has been around for ten years and is still available, much to my surprise.
Thinking Forth: A Language and Philosophy for Solving Problems
Leo Brodie, 1984
Yes, another book about Forth.
But this one is worth reading less for the Forth and more because it's one of the few books about how to decompose problems and structure code. You'd think this book was written by Fowler and friends, until you realize it's from the mid-1980s. That Brodie uses "factor" (which originated in the Forth community) instead of "refactor" is also a giveaway. What's impressive here is there's no OOP, no discussion of patterns, no heavy terminology. It's a book about understanding what you're trying to achieve, avoiding redundancy, and writing dead simple code.
It's worth it for the Forth, too, especially the interspersed bits of wisdom from experts, including Forth creator Chuck Moore.
permalink February 18, 2008
I'm James Hague, a recovering programmer who has been designing video games since the 1980s. Programming Without Being Obsessed With Programming and Organizational Skills Beat Algorithmic Wizardry are good starting points. For the older stuff, try the 2012 Retrospective.

articles.title: Ask HN: How did you convince family and friends to join your XMPP/Matrix server?
articles.body:
I love open-source software and open protocols, but my family and friends primarily communicate through SMS for exactly the reasons in https://xkcd.com/2365/
Whenever XMPP or Matrix threads pop up on HN, several commenters casually mention their "friends and family XMPP (or Matrix) server."
How did you convince friends and family to move away from SMS/WhatsApp and replace it with a niche messaging app?
My family and friends aren't hardcore nerdy, but they're more tech-savvy than average. Their needs in messaging are mainly pragmatic: they want ease of use, reliability, and fun features. They don't care that much about privacy, decentralization, or extensibility (though I care about those things a lot).
I've been experimenting with self-hosting XMPP and Matrix servers and clients in the past week, and the UX is even worse than I expected. It seems like all the clients either imitate Slack, imitate Discord, or imitate hot garbage. I haven't seen any that try to be a simple, friendly replacement for SMS. I'm a software developer who uses computers all day, and I find the UX for most of the clients incredibly hard to use.
The only angle I could see to pitch XMPP/Matrix to people for non-philosophical reasons are that there's a more consistent experience across iOS/Android. The biggest shortcoming I think is visible to regular users is that there's feature degradation and missing information when iOS users have SMS conversations with Android users, especially in group chats.
For people who have successfully won family and friends to XMPP or Matrix, what was your pitch? What do you recommend others do to make XMPP or Matrix an attractive experience for a regular person?

articles.title: 19 Easy Corn Recipes
articles.body:
Corn has quite the résumé for a humble grocery staple. It’s sweet and juicy straight off the cob in summer, but hand me a bag of frozen kernels, a can of corn, or a little cornmeal once the weather cools down, and I am still very much interested. I’m talking golden cornbread, creamy Thanksgiving sides, smoky street corn salads, and even a risotto that makes use of those leftover cobs (yes, really!). These 19 easy corn recipes prove you can get a LOT of mileage out of this affordable ingredient long after fresh corn season wraps up!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
Cornbread Recipes Worth Saving Room For
There’s always a good reason to bake a batch of cornbread. It’s sweet, tender, and so very inexpensive to make. The basic recipe is already pretty wonderful, but throw in some cheese, sweet potato, or a drizzle of spicy honey, and suddenly you’ve got a whole new reason to make another batch.
1. Homemade Cornbread
Easy Homemade Cornbread Recipe
The OG. The one everybody should have in their back pocket! Our homemade cornbread is made entirely from scratch with a handful of pantry staples, and it takes just 30 minutes from start to finish. It’s lightly sweet, beautifully tender, and honestly, I could eat a warm slice with butter any time of day. If you don’t know, now you know. 😉
2. Sweet Potato Cornbread
Sweet Potato Cornbread
Can we talk about just how good this sweet potato cornbread is?! Mashed sweet potato and sour cream make the crumb extra rich and moist, while a little cinnamon and nutmeg give it the most delicious warmth. It’s sweeter and denser than traditional cornbread, and I love serving it with a big bowl of smoky bean chili.
3. Chili Cheese Cornbread
Chili Cheese Cornbread
This one takes the shortcut route, and I’m not mad at it. Two boxes of cornbread mix get a serious flavor upgrade with chili powder, sweet corn kernels, and a generous layer of shredded cheddar. The result is a slightly spicy, cheesy chili cheese cornbread that’s ready in about 30 minutes.
4. Hot Honey Cornbread
Hot Honey Cornbread
Remember when hot honey was having a moment? Yeah, I’m still not over it. 😋 This hot honey cornbread takes sweet, buttery cornbread and gives it a little kick with a warm honey-butter drizzle and red pepper flakes. Sour cream keeps the inside deliciously soft and cake-like, and that drizzle of sweet heat makes it an excellent partner for savory dinners.
Thanksgiving Staples
Corn comes in many delicious disguises at Thanksgiving! From rich and creamy to fluffy and golden, there’s plenty to love about these classic holiday sides. Better yet, they’re made with affordable ingredients, so you can put on a delicious spread without blowing your holiday grocery budget.
5. Corn Pudding
Corn Pudding
Soft, creamy, cheesy, and just sweet enough to keep you coming back for another spoonful. This homemade corn pudding is somewhere between a savory custard and a very soft cornbread, with juicy corn kernels suspended in a rich mixture of eggs, half-and-half, sour cream, and cheddar. It’s made completely from scratch, with no boxed mixes or canned creamed corn! Frozen corn also keeps things convenient and brings the cost down to around $0.80 per serving.
6. Creamed Corn
Creamed Corn Recipe
I’m officially voting to leave the canned cream-style corn on the grocery store shelf this Thanksgiving! My homemade creamed corn is buttery and silky, with sweet corn and finished with Parmesan cheese for extra savory flavor. I make a simple roux to thicken the sauce, and frozen corn works just as well as fresh. The whole thing takes only 25 minutes, costs about $0.66 per serving, and is SO much tastier than anything from a can.
7. Cornbread Dressing
Cornbread Dressing
If you’re looking to change things up from traditional bread stuffing, give this Southern-style cornbread dressing a try. Crumbled homemade cornbread and toasted white bread soak up a flavorful mixture of broth, butter, sautéed vegetables, and herbs before baking until golden. It’s savory, moist, and slightly crumbly, with those lovely crisp bits around the edges. Better yet, one batch makes 12 generous servings, so it’s a smart choice when you’re feeding a crowd!
8. Cornbread Casserole
Cornbread Casserole
Two Thanksgiving sides, one baking dish. Now THAT is holiday cooking I can get behind! This cornbread casserole combines whole corn kernels, cream-style corn, cheddar, and boxed cornbread mix for a rich, buttery bake with a soft, creamy middle and a lightly crisp, golden top. It’s a little more substantial than corn pudding, but much softer than regular cornbread. I love how it’s an affordable way to get two favorites onto the table at once.
A Little Taste of Summer
There’s nothing quite like fresh sweet corn in the summertime, especially when the ears are piled high at the farmers market or on sale at the grocery store! That’s usually when you’ll find the best flavor and prices, so I like taking full advantage. These recipes make those fresh kernels shine, but you’ll find a few clever frozen corn options in the mix, too.
9. Cowboy Caviar
Cowboy Caviar
A bowl of cowboy caviar never lasts long once the tortilla chips come out! This colorful dip starts with inexpensive black beans and black-eyed peas, then adds crunchy vegetables and a zesty homemade lime dressing. I highly recommend stirring in some fresh or thawed frozen corn for extra sweetness and crunch. It’s a low-cost way to stretch the batch, and any leftovers are delicious spooned over tacos, salads, or rice bowls.
10. Street Corn Salad
Street Corn Salad (Esquites)
All the tangy, creamy, spicy flavors of Mexican street corn, minus the messy cob! I quickly char fresh corn kernels in a hot skillet to give my street corn salad that delicious roasted flavor, then toss them with cotija cheese, cilantro, and a creamy chili-lime dressing. It’s inspired by elote and esquites, and this salad is ALWAYS on repeat at my house during the summer.
11. Sweet Corn Fritters
Sweet Corn Fritters
Crispy golden edges, soft centers, little bursts of sweet corn, and salty feta cheese. Need I say more?! These sweet corn fritters are a delicious little appetizer, snack, or light lunch, especially with a dollop of sour cream or aioli for dipping. I make them with fresh corn when it’s in season, but frozen works too! Just make sure you thaw and dry the kernels thoroughly before frying to avoid excess oil splatter.
12. Street Corn Pasta Salad
Elote (Street Corn) Pasta Salad
My street corn salad has a pasta-loving cousin, and it’s this elote-inspired pasta salad! This easy recipe mixes tender ditalini with charred corn, poblano peppers, queso fresco, and a creamy chipotle-lime dressing. It has all those smoky, tangy, cheesy flavors I love, but with pasta to make it a little more filling. You can also prep it ahead for potlucks and cookouts. Plus, using frozen corn helps keep the cost at a very reasonable $0.69 per serving.
13. Sweet Corn Salsa
Sweet Corn Salsa
No cooking required for this one! Raw sweet corn is surprisingly juicy and crunchy, and it’s absolutely delicious tossed with ripe tomatoes, jalapeño, red onion, cilantro, and lime. This fresh sweet corn salsa takes just 15 minutes to make, and it’s fantastic with tortilla chips or piled onto tacos. If you’ve only ever eaten cooked corn, this is your sign to try something different.
14. Sweet Corn Risotto
Sweet Corn Risotto
Here’s a little kitchen thrift I can fully get behind…don’t throw away those corn cobs! For my sweet corn risotto, I use the stripped cobs to infuse the cooking broth with extra sweetness and earthy corn flavor. The tender kernels add a lovely contrast to the creamy Arborio rice, butter, and Parmesan cheese. It’s rich and comforting without needing any heavy cream, and using every last bit of the corn makes it even more satisfying to prepare.
Corn + Zucchini: A Very Good Match
Corn and zucchini come into season around the same time, which is handy when your garden (or the farmers market!) is overflowing with both. Sweet corn gives zucchini a lovely pop of flavor and texture, and together they can make everything from a hearty baked pie to a crunchy raw salad. If you’ve still got more squash to use, our zucchini recipes roundup has plenty of other ideas, too!
15. Sweet Corn and Zucchini Pie
Sweet Corn and Zucchini Pie
Who needs a pastry crust when the filling is this good?! This sweet corn and zucchini pie combines fresh corn, zucchini, yellow squash, eggs, cottage cheese, and mozzarella into a creamy bake. No pastry crust means less time and money, and one pie makes six generous servings for about $1.21 each. I’d happily put this on the table for brunch, lunch, or a light dinner.
16. Sweet Corn Salad
Summer Sweet Corn Salad
Don’t overlook the zucchini hiding in this sweet corn salad. It adds a lovely fresh crunch alongside raw sweet corn, juicy tomatoes, creamy avocado, and tender little pasta shells. Everything gets tossed in a bright lemon-Dijon vinaigrette, and the pasta makes it substantial enough for a satisfying lunch.
17. Zucchini, Corn, and Toasted Almond Salad
Zucchini, Corn, and Toasted Almond Salad
A textural wonderland, truly! I leave both the zucchini AND sweet corn raw in my zucchini, corn, and toasted almond salad, which keeps everything wonderfully fresh and crisp. Toasted almonds add a buttery crunch, ribbons of Parmesan bring a little saltiness, and a homemade lemon-mint dressing ties it all together. There’s no need to heat the oven, it’s ready in 25 minutes, and each serving costs just $0.99!
Corn on the Cob
Sometimes, a little butter and salt are all sweet corn really needs. You can let the grill do its thing for that lovely summer flavor or take the quick and easy route with the microwave. Either method gives you juicy, tender kernels without much fuss, so pick whichever suits your day.
18. Grilled Corn on the Cob
Grilled Corn on the Cob
I’ve loved corn on the cob since I was a kid, and grilling it is still one of my favorite ways to enjoy it. For my grilled corn on the cob, I soak the ears and cook them right in their husks, letting the corn steam inside while the outside gets beautifully charred. There’s no need to buy aluminum foil, so that’s one less thing to spend money on or throw away! A grill pan also works when cooking outdoors isn’t an option.
19. Microwave Corn on the Cob
Microwave Corn On The Cob
Four minutes per ear, give or take your microwave’s wattage. That’s all it takes to make perfectly juicy microwave corn on the cob! The corn steams right in its husk, so you don’t need to boil a big pot of water. Add a little butter and salt, and you’ve got one of the easiest corn side dishes imaginable.

articles.title: Chainalysis Says Breach Exposed Credentials For All Customers
articles.body:
Chainalysis Says Breach Exposed Credentials For All Customers (bleepingcomputer.com) 3
			
		 	
				Chainalysis says attackers exposed usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all of its customers. "While the company locked Chainalysis accounts as a precaution after discovering that some customers' passwords had been exposed and asked users to reset their passwords before signing in again, it has now taken the login portal offline, together with Reactor and Data Solutions, the Know-Your-Transaction (KYT) user interface and API, and address screening products, after discovering further abnormal activity," reports BleepingComputer.
The company says it has no evidence that investigative data or blockchain attribution records were accessed or altered, but all users will be required to reset passwords and rotate API keys before regaining access. BleepingComputer reports:  Chainalysis provides blockchain analysis tools to trace cryptocurrency transactions and investigate crimes such as fraud, ransomware, and money laundering. Its customer list includes law enforcement, government agencies, financial institutions, insurance companies, and cryptocurrency businesses worldwide. This follows the company's disclosure last Friday that attackers using AI tools accessed customers' names, email addresses, user IDs, and organizational role labels using what it described as "offensive agentic techniques."
While it initially said the impact was limited and the breach affected only non-sensitive identity metadata, later updates revealed that usernames and password hashes for all customers were exposed in an "on-path attack" (more commonly known as a Man-in-the-Middle or MITM attack). However, the company found no evidence that the attackers accessed investigative graph data or altered its blockchain attribution repositories. [...] To ensure threat actors don't access affected accounts, Chainalysis asked customers to provide trusted IP addresses so they can regain access to the login portal once it is brought back online and reset their credentials.

articles.title: Christopher Ward C63 Sealander Extreme GMT, black dial and ceramic bezel, on an orange Cordura strap
articles.body:
I was watching a snarky YouTube video where a watch influencer was ranking all watch brands. He labeled Christopher Ward his favorite emerging indie brand. So here we go.
It’s got Tudor-esque chonk on both the markers and the hands. The ceramic bezel is a work of art — one of those you have to feel with your hands. The face, the asphalt vibes of a Patek, is compelling. I am a known sucker for a splash of orange, and there are multiple splashes to love. V-strap? Possible mistake. Jury is out.

articles.title: Activists Breach Microsoft Data Center Construction Site As Protests Spread In Europe
articles.body:
Activists Breach Microsoft Data Center Construction Site As Protests Spread In Europe (yahoo.com) 54
			
		 	
				More than 100 activists breached a Microsoft AI data center construction site in Amsterdam as part of coordinated protests against the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. "These data centres are destroying our world. It's becoming uninhabitable because of all the resources they consume. That's why we're here today," protester Sam van der Beek said. Reuters reports:  Activist groups have announced actions in 16 countries on Friday and Saturday, according to the "Stop Dirty Data Centers" coalition, which is rallying environmental groups and digital rights campaigns behind calls to pause large-scale construction. In Amsterdam on Friday, more than 100 activists gathered at the construction site of a Microsoft AI data centre, marching arm in arm before breaking into the site, climbing cranes, hanging balloons and dancing while police stood by. Some carried placards with messages reading: "Screw your datacenter."
Site owner Pure Data Centers, which plans to invest more than $1 billion and is backed by Brookfield-owned Oaktree, said it was committed to engagement with local stakeholders. "We respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have," it said. Other planned actions include a march in Dublin, a protest outside the parliament building in Warsaw, and a demonstration against a different Microsoft data centre in Denmark. [...] Stop Dirty Data Centers says it is not anti-progress or calling for existing data centers to be closed but that major construction should be halted until governments establish clearer rules.

articles.title: Show HN: Agents infer Lego mechanisms from sources, then animate them
articles.body:
Give an LDraw LEGO© model to an AI agent, get back a Blender-animated version of it.
The agent will:
- Reverse-engineer (infer) the LDraw model's mechanics from its .mpd source code file 🤓
- Study the discovered mechanisms.
- Plan the interactions between their different mechanical components.
- And finally, turn those plans into python code for Blender, that will:
  - Create the required rigs for controlling the different mechanisms.
  - Animate them according to plan! 🤯
Take a look at the ▶ HOWTO video!
Note
The installation process will install every required tool and dependency locally on this project repo, in order to avoid polluting the host OS.
However, there is a requirement of setting several env vars on rc files, like e.g. .bashrc or .zshrc
The installed dependencies, like e.g. Blender, are git-ignored by default.
You'll need Python 3.12+ installed.
Start by cloning the repo and running the setup script, pick the right one for your OS:
git clone https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha.git
cd ldraw-mecha
./setup-macos.sh            # or ./setup-linux.sh, ./setup-win-wsl.sh
At the end of the setup process, you'll get a snippet with the env vars to be added to your shell profile (.bashrc, .zshrc, etc.), something like e.g.:
# >>> ldraw-mecha (from setup-macos.sh) >>>
export LDRAW_DIR="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw"
export LDRAWDIR="$LDRAW_DIR"
export BLENDER_BIN="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender"
export LEOCAD="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/LeoCAD.app/Contents/MacOS/LeoCAD"
export LDRAW_XRAY_CACHE="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/.cache/ldraw-xray"
export LDRAW_ANNOTATOR_DB="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw-info.db"
# export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...   # optional: Jev semantic search (jev-rerank)
# other env vars...
# <<< ldraw-mecha <<<
If you're on VS Code or a terminal, restart it in order to get an updated env with the newly added env vars.
For inspecting and selecting one pre-annotated model to animate, open the annotated models selector by running:
python3 model-selector/serve.py
Then, take a look at the ▶ HOWTO video for a step-by-step usage example.
Note
More samples available at: Gallery
Animations have been generated from original models, not from ai-generated ones.
These are some samples of animations by different agents, take a look at their Summaries for more details.
- Agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5
- Original model: 42043-1_Flatbed-Trailer.mpd
- Context: The model was too large and complex for fully animating it, finally I accepted Sonnet's suggestion about animating the crane alone.
Original
- Agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5
- Original model: 3625-1.mpd
- Context: Asked for an in-place animation, to avoid the plane moving around.
- Agent: Claude Opus 5.5
- Original model: None
- Context: This one is actually a generated composition, from several different minifigs, to be used as a "howto reference" for other agents also animating minifigs.
After publishing LDraw Nova, a sibling project for agentic generation of LDraw models, several people reached out to me asking about if models could be animated somehow.
During the development of Nova, I noticed that adding some special annotations to .mpd original model source files, and then giving those to agents, would:
- Help agents in understanding how to build other different models.
- But also, in understanding how a model was built.
Which gave me the idea that, maybe, an agent would also understand how a model would work.
As a first step to it, I gave annotated models to different agents, and prompted them to infer (reverse-engineer) their constituent submodels (see Haiku 5.5. experiment below).
Results from inference experiments were both pretty good and consistent across different agents, and I also noticed the following: many of the submodels inferred were actually mechanisms.
After questioning several agents about those inferred mechanisms, regarding how would they actually work, I also got consistent results: agents would describe behaviours based on the descriptions for the parts on a mechanism! 🤯
At this point, I had the following:
- Agents would split and refine models into submodels and mechanisms.
- Agents would understand each mechanism in isolation.
- Agents would understand how individual mechanisms worked.
The result of an actual divide-and-conquer process, right? 🤓
Which would make handling individual mechanisms manageable. 🤩
Now, there was the matter of giving agents the means to actually animate mechanisms they already knew how they worked.
I was playing with Blender MCP at the time, and Blender looked promising as a tool that would provide agents a way to manipulate LDraw models in 3D, imported into Blender as glTF (.glb) files.
But there was still an open issue:
How to map from a refined model source code an agent would understand, to its equivalent 3D model in glTF format an agent could manipulate?
And the solution I found was:
Annotate the 3D glTF model's nodes with the same annotations as the source code, so the agent would:
- Outside Blender: plan on submodels 🤔 and parts as source code.
- Inside Blender: execute on matching nodes ✨ on the 3D glTF model.
Now, I had a draft for a process, but no tools for the agent to use and carry it forward.
Given that the process would require a high amount of complex geometric and spatial calculations, I asked the agent to derive a new python toolset from the one created for ldraw-nova
The new python toolset I refined iteratively, by giving the agent simple models at the beginning, and increasingly complex ones each time.
And to test it, I gave an agent instructions to:
- first, plan from an annotated and refined .mpd model
- then, generate a glTF 3D version of it, with matching annotations
- then, upload it to Blender
- and then, produce the Blender python scripts that would animate the model as planned.
And it finally worked! 🚀🚀🚀
(but not perfectly) 😜

This is not an executable code fragment, but more like a 3D CAD model fragment written in LDraw language.
Infer what this submodel is, and also split it into submodels (starting with: 0 FILE):
- always with relevant, semantical meaning,
- the first 0-line following every 0 FILE line is the "description line" for the submodel, according to the LDaw standard
- add the description for every submodel there, a one-liner, as a person would describe it while looking at it
- at the answer, first place the parent model, then the child one(s) and then the grandchildren, and then descendants... etc.: go from containers or parents to containees or children, children of children. etc.

- Complex mechanisms and large models take too much time and effort to animate.

- LDCad and Shadow Library, Roland Melkert.
- pyldraw3's Harold Martin (@hbmartin), and contributors.
... and thanks to all of the many other LDraw creators!

There is a lot amazing people that generously contributed to this, even for decades, by generously donating their finest work to the public domain and open source community.
